eras.note: Bahia stayed loyal to the Portuguese crown when independence was declared on 7 September 1822, and the Portuguese were expelled only on 2 July 1823, so 1822-23 documents from Salvador are Portuguese-held rather than imperial.

eras.polity: Brazil — State of Bahia, State of Sergipe
eras.note: Bahia became a state in 1889. Decreto 9.886 of 7 March 1888 set up general civil registration, in force from 1 January 1889 according to a registry association's account; uptake was slow in the interior, where distance from the registry offices held registration down.

regions.label: Pernambuco, Alagoas, Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte — the sugar coast
regions.sub: Recife, Olinda, Maceió, João Pessoa, Natal, Penedo

eras.polity: Captaincy of Pernambuco (Duarte Coelho) with Alagoas inside it
eras.note: King John III created the hereditary captaincies in 1534 and Pernambuco went to Duarte Coelho, who arrived in 1535. Alagoas was part of the Pernambuco captaincy until 1817.

The Dutch held Olinda by 16 February 1630 and Recife by early March, and made Mauritsstad, on the island of António Vaz, their capital. Recife fell to the Portuguese in January 1654 (26 or 28 January depending on the source). The Dutch West India Company's records, including papers from Dutch Brazil for 1630-54, are in the Oude WIC archive at the Nationaal Archief (1.05.01.01).
The central settlement of the Palmares quilombo, in what is now Alagoas, was destroyed on 6 February 1694. In 1710 the Mascate War broke out between Recife's merchants and Olinda's sugar planters.

eras.polity: United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves
eras.note: The Pernambuco revolt of 1817 was suppressed within two months, and Alagoas was made a separate captaincy in 1817 as a reprisal.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — provinces of Pernambuco, Alagoas, Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte
eras.note: Alagoas became a province in 1822 and its capital moved from the town of Alagoas to Maceió in 1839. FamilySearch lists civil-registration collections for Pernambuco (1804-2016) and Rio Grande do Norte (1803-2020); the ranges include records earlier than general civil registration.

eras.polity: Brazil — states of Pernambuco, Alagoas, Paraíba, Rio Grande do Norte
eras.note: The provinces became states with the Republic in 1889, the year Brazil's general civil registry began under the decree of 1888.

regions.label: Maranhão, Piauí and Ceará — São Luís, Fortaleza, Teresina
regions.sub: São Luís, Fortaleza, Teresina, Sobral, Parnaíba, Imperatriz

eras.note: The French founded Equinoctial France on the island of São Luís in 1612 after a first trading expedition in 1594. The Portuguese expelled them in 1615; the Ceará article dates the expulsion from Ceará and Maranhão to 1612.
Ceará, Maranhão and Pará were united in 1621 as the Estado do Maranhão, a colonial state that stayed separate from the rest of Brazil until the 1770s.

eras.polity: Dutch Brazil — Ceará and São Luís
eras.note: The Dutch took Fort São Sebastião in Ceará in 1637 and held São Luís from 1641 to 1644. Their rule in Brazil ended in 1654.

eras.polity: Estado do Maranhão, then Estado do Grão-Pará e Maranhão
eras.note: Ceará was a dependency of Pernambuco from 1680 until 1799, so Ceará was governed through Pernambuco in those years. Piauí was split off from Maranhão in 1759. The Estado do Maranhão is dated 1621-1751 and the Estado do Grão-Pará e Maranhão 1751-1772 in the list of captaincies.

eras.polity: Captaincies of Maranhão and Piauí; Ceará independent from 1799
eras.note: The separate colonial state ended in 1772 on the list of captaincies and in 1774 on the Maranhão article, when it came under Brazil's colonial administration again. Ceará became an independent captaincy in 1799.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — provinces of Maranhão, Piauí and Ceará
eras.note: Maranhão did not join the declaration of independence in 1822; Lord Cochrane drove out the Portuguese in 1823. Ceará became a province in 1822, rose in a republican revolt in 1824, and was the first province to abolish slavery, on 25 March 1884. The Great Drought in Ceará is dated 1877-80.

eras.polity: Brazil — states of Maranhão, Piauí and Ceará
eras.note: General civil registration under the 1888 decree took effect on 1 January 1889 according to a registry association; in the interior, Church control and distance from notary offices held registration rates down.

regions.label: Pará, Amazonas, Amapá, Roraima, Acre and Rondônia — the Amazon
regions.sub: Belém, Manaus, Santarém, Macapá, Rio Branco, Porto Velho

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Captaincy of Grão-Pará in the Estado do Maranhão
eras.note: Belém was founded in January 1616 as the Fort of the Nativity, and the captaincy of Grão-Pará was created that year as part of the Estado do Maranhão. The list of captaincies gives 1652 as the year Pará became independent of Maranhão.

eras.polity: Estado do Grão-Pará e Maranhão; Captaincy of São José do Rio Negro
eras.note: The Captaincy of São José do Rio Negro was created in March 1755 under Pará, with its seat at Mariuá (now Barcelos). In 1808 the capital moved to Barra do Rio Negro, which was renamed Manaus in 1832.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Pará
eras.note: Pará joined independent Brazil in 1823. The Cabanagem revolt ran from 1835 to January 1840; the Amazon region stayed loyal to the imperial government.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — provinces of Pará and Amazonas
eras.note: Pedro II created the Province of Amazonas in 1850, separating it from Pará. FamilySearch's Pará civil-registration collection spans 1815-1995.

eras.polity: Brazil — Pará and Amazonas; Acre contested with Bolivia
eras.note: Bolivia claimed Acre after the border of 1867, Peru also claimed it, and Brazilian rubber settlers kept moving in. The Acre War ran from 1899 to 1903.

eras.polity: Brazil — Pará, Amazonas, Amapá, Roraima, Rondônia, Acre
eras.note: The Treaty of Petrópolis of 17 November 1903 transferred Acre from Bolivia to Brazil; the Territory of Acre was created in 1904 and became a state on 15 June 1962. Acre's status before 1903 was disputed between Bolivia, Peru and Brazil.

regions.label: Rio de Janeiro — the bay, the Paraíba valley and the capital
regions.sub: Rio de Janeiro, Niterói, Petrópolis, Paraty, Campos dos Goytacazes, Volta Redonda

eras.note: The French occupied the bay from 1555 to 1567. Estácio de Sá founded the city of Rio de Janeiro in March 1565 to prevent French occupation.

eras.polity: Captaincy of Rio de Janeiro — southern government of Brazil
eras.note: A dual government was set up in 1572, with a northern seat at Salvador and a southern one at Rio de Janeiro.
Rio became the capital of the colony in 1763. São Paulo was under the governor of Rio from 1748 to 1765.

eras.polity: Portuguese court in Rio — United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves
eras.note: The Portuguese court moved to Rio in 1808 and the Casa da Suplicação, the court of last instance, was set up there by a decree of 10 May 1808. The Arquivo Nacional holds a Casa da Suplicação do Brasil fund, transferred from the Corte de Apelação in 1912.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Neutral Municipality (city) and Province of Rio de Janeiro
eras.note: In 1834 the city became a neutral city and capital, while the province of Rio de Janeiro had its seat in Niterói; city and province were therefore separate jurisdictions. The Arquivo Nacional was created in 1838 as the Imperial Public Archives. FamilySearch's Rio de Janeiro civil-registration collection spans 1829-2012.

eras.polity: Brazil — Federal District (Rio) and State of Rio de Janeiro
eras.note: In 1889 the city became the Federal District and the province a state. Petrópolis was the state capital from 1894 to 1902, after which Niterói regained the role. Civil-registration offices were created under the 1888 decree, with the service dated to 1 January 1889.

eras.polity: Brazil — State of Guanabara (1960-75), then State of Rio de Janeiro
eras.note: When the federal capital moved to Brasília in 1960 the city became the State of Guanabara. Guanabara merged with Rio de Janeiro state in 1975 and the former city-state became a municipality.

regions.label: Espírito Santo — Vitória and the Doce valley
regions.sub: Vitória, Vila Velha, Serra, Guarapari, Colatina, Linhares

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Hereditary captaincy of Espírito Santo (Vasco Coutinho)
eras.note: Vasco Coutinho arrived on 23 May 1535. Vitória was founded on 8 September 1551 after Vila Velha, the first capital, proved vulnerable to raids. The captaincy became independent of Bahia only in 1799.
Brazil became a kingdom in 1815 and Espírito Santo became a province in 1821.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Espírito Santo
eras.note: Santa Isabel, the first German settlement, was founded in 1844, and Dutch settlers from Zeeuws-Vlaanderen arrived between 1858 and 1862.
The first elected governor took office on 7 June 1891. The decree creating general civil registration is dated 7 March 1888; its start is given as 1 January 1889.

regions.label: São Paulo — São Vicente, Piratininga and the coffee lands
regions.sub: São Paulo, Santos, São Vicente, Campinas, Sorocaba, Ribeirão Preto

eras.note: São Vicente, founded in 1532, was the first permanent Portuguese settlement in the Americas. A Jesuit mission on the site of the city of São Paulo was established on 25 January 1554. The bandeirantes expanded the colony into the interior in the 17th century.

eras.polity: Captaincy of São Paulo and Minas de Ouro
eras.note: The captaincy of 1709 followed disputes over gold-mining territory and included the mining region that became Minas Gerais in 1720.

eras.polity: Captaincy of São Paulo — under Rio from 1748
eras.note: Santa Catarina split from São Paulo in 1738 (the list of captaincies shows 1738 or 1739). In 1748 Goiás and Mato Grosso were separated and São Paulo was placed under the governor of Rio.

eras.polity: Captaincy of São Paulo — autonomous again
eras.note: The captaincy regained its autonomy in 1765. The Arquivo Público do Estado de São Paulo holds its government records, entered in UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2015. Lages and its district passed to Santa Catarina in 1820.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of São Paulo
eras.note: The territory of today's Paraná, the fifth comarca of Curitiba, was part of the province until 1853.

Coffee took off in the 1880s; Italian immigration began in the late 19th century, Japanese from 1908, and foreigners were over 55% of the state's population by 1893. FamilySearch's São Paulo civil-registration collection spans 1925-1995; the decree of 7 March 1888 made civil registration universal.

regions.label: Paraná — Curitiba, Paranaguá, Guaíra
regions.sub: Curitiba, Paranaguá, Ponta Grossa, Londrina, Foz do Iguaçu, Guaíra

eras.polity: Coast under São Vicente; Guaíra on the Spanish side
eras.note: Domingo Martínez de Irala founded Ontiveros in 1554 near the Guaíra Falls, and Jesuit reductions were opened in the west and south-west, which largely belonged to the Spanish crown. Portuguese colonisation was mostly confined to the coast.

eras.polity: Captaincy of São Paulo — comarca of Paranaguá and Curitiba
eras.note: In 1811 residents of Paranaguá asked for a new province separate from the captaincy of São Paulo; the request was not granted.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of São Paulo, fifth comarca of Curitiba
eras.note: Until 1853 this ground was governed from São Paulo.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Paraná
eras.note: Imperial Law 704 of 29 August 1853 created the province from the fifth comarca of São Paulo; it was installed on 19 December 1853 with Curitiba as capital. Italian, German, Polish and Ukrainian immigration grew in the mid-19th century.
The Contestado War ran from October 1912 to August 1916, over land claimed by both Paraná and Santa Catarina. On 12 October 1916 the two governors signed an agreement.

The north was settled in the 1940s by the expansion of São Paulo's coffee, and the south-east by migrants from Rio Grande do Sul. Universal civil registration dates from the decree of 7 March 1888; FamilySearch notes that some areas have civil records from the 1860s and 1870s and others only from the 1920s.

regions.label: Santa Catarina — Desterro, Joinville, Blumenau, Lages
regions.sub: Florianópolis, Joinville, Blumenau, Laguna, São Francisco do Sul, Lages

eras.note: Before registers. Sebastian Cabot named the island of Santa Catarina in 1526.
São Francisco do Sul was founded in 1658, Nossa Senhora do Desterro (Florianópolis) in 1675 and Laguna in 1676.

The captaincy was founded in 1738 and incorporated into Rio de Janeiro's in 1739. About 5,000 Azorean settlers arrived between 1748 and 1756. Spanish troops occupied and destroyed the island's settlement in 1777.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Santa Catarina
eras.note: Rebels proclaimed the Juliana Republic at Laguna in July 1839 during the Ragamuffin War. Dona Francisca (Joinville) was founded in 1850, Blumenau in 1852 and Brusque in 1860.

eras.polity: Brazil — State of Santa Catarina; Contestado disputed with Paraná
eras.note: The Contestado War began in 1912 over land claimed by both states, and the conflict and the dispute ended in 1916.
From the 1950s Italian-Brazilian settlers from Rio Grande do Sul were encouraged to colonise the far west and centre of the state.

regions.label: Rio Grande do Sul — Porto Alegre, São Leopoldo, Caxias, the Missões
regions.sub: Porto Alegre, São Leopoldo, Caxias do Sul, Rio Grande, Pelotas, Santo Ângelo

eras.polity: Spanish Jesuit reductions (Misiones Orientales) and the Portuguese frontier
eras.note: The Jesuits refounded seven reductions in the east of the Missions in 1687. The Treaty of Madrid of 13 January 1750 settled the boundaries between Spain's and Portugal's colonies; Guaraní resistance continued until 1756.

eras.polity: Spanish occupation of the town of Rio Grande
eras.note: Spanish forces occupied the town of Rio Grande from 1763 to 1776.

eras.polity: Rio Grande de São Pedro (Portuguese coast); the Missões Spanish
eras.note: The Treaty of San Ildefonso of 1777 gave the coastal region to Portugal and the Missões to Spain. The captaincy of Rio Grande do Sul is dated 1760 on the list of captaincies.

eras.polity: Captaincy of São Pedro do Rio Grande
eras.note: The Badajoz treaty of 1801 handed the Missões to the Portuguese; the Sete Povos were captured that year.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of São Pedro do Rio Grande do Sul
eras.note: German immigrants first arrived in 1824, and São Leopoldo was the first city they settled. The Ragamuffin War ran from 20 September 1835 and ended with the Ponche Verde treaty in 1845. Italian immigration began in 1875 and continued until 1914.

eras.polity: Brazil — State of Rio Grande do Sul
eras.note: Civil registration followed the 1888 decree and was in force from 1889; the Arquivo Público do Estado do Rio Grande do Sul is the state archive.

regions.label: Minas Gerais — the gold and diamond country
regions.sub: Ouro Preto, Mariana, Diamantina, Belo Horizonte, Montes Claros, Uberlândia

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: São Paulo and Minas de Ouro — the gold rush
eras.note: Gold was found in 1692-93, on the Carmo River in 1696 and at Itacolomi in 1698, the start of Vila Rica (now Ouro Preto). The War of the Emboabas ran from 1707 to 1709.

The captaincy was created after the Vila Rica revolt of 1720, separate from São Paulo, so earlier events in the mining region fall under São Paulo. Diamonds were found in the 1720s in the Jequitinhonha valley, around Tijuco (now Diamantina). The Inconfidência Mineira conspiracy failed in 1789.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Minas Gerais
eras.note: The seat of government was Ouro Preto (formerly Vila Rica), replaced by Belo Horizonte in the 1890s.
Belo Horizonte was inaugurated on 12 December 1897 as Cidade de Minas, replacing Ouro Preto as the capital, and was renamed in 1906. Civil registers date from the 1888 decree, in force from 1889.

regions.label: Goiás, Tocantins and the Federal District
regions.sub: Goiás (Velho), Goiânia, Brasília, Anápolis, Palmas, Catalão

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Interior of the São Paulo captaincy — mining frontier
eras.note: Bartolomeu Bueno da Silva found gold in 1682, and his settlement became Goiás Velho; the date is contested. Gold discoveries in Cuiabá and Goiás made São Paulo a hub of trade with the interior.
Goiás was split from São Paulo in 1748 on the list of captaincies; the Goiás article dates the captaincy to 1744.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Goiás
eras.note: Goiás became a province of the empire in 1822.

Goiânia was planned in 1933 to replace the old capital, the state government moved there in 1937 and the city was inaugurated in 1942. General civil registration is dated to 1889, under a decree of 1888.

eras.polity: Brazil — State of Goiás, Federal District, State of Tocantins (from 1988)
eras.note: The federal government officially moved to Brasília in 1960, the site having been chosen in 1956. In 1988 the northern half of Goiás became the separate state of Tocantins.

regions.label: Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul — Cuiabá, Corumbá, Campo Grande
regions.sub: Cuiabá, Cáceres, Corumbá, Campo Grande, Vila Bela da Santíssima Trindade, Dourados

eras.polity: Western interior of the São Paulo captaincy
eras.note: Gold discoveries in Cuiabá made São Paulo a hub for trade between the coast, the River Plate region and the interior.
Mato Grosso was separated from São Paulo in 1748, the same year as Goiás.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Mato Grosso
eras.note: Mato Grosso was a province of the empire from independence until 1889.
The 1888 decree introduced civil registration, effective 1889.

eras.polity: Brazil — State of Mato Grosso (south-west part ceded to Bolivia, 1903)
eras.note: The Treaty of Petrópolis of 17 November 1903, which gave Acre to Brazil, ceded the south-western part of Mato Grosso to Bolivia in exchange. The state was one unit until 1977.

eras.polity: Brazil — States of Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul
eras.note: The state was split in 1977, creating Mato Grosso do Sul, so a place in Mato Grosso do Sul belonged to Mato Grosso until then.

regions.label: Córdoba — the Argentine heartland
regions.sub: Córdoba, Río Cuarto, Alta Gracia, Villa María, Villa Dolores

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Córdoba de la Nueva Andalucía
eras.note: Córdoba was founded on 6 July 1573 as a midpoint on the route to the Río de la Plata. The Jesuit Colegio de Monserrat dates from 1599 and the university from 1613. Crown correspondence for the Indies is held in the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, much of it digitised through PARES.

eras.polity: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata — Intendancy of Córdoba del Tucumán
eras.note: The viceroyalty was created in 1776. The Intendancy of Córdoba del Tucumán was created in 1783, with Rafael de Sobremonte as its first governor, as the capital of a territory that also took in La Rioja, Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis. Records of Cuyo and La Rioja in these years can therefore sit with Córdoba's.

eras.polity: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata — Córdoba under its own governors
eras.note: After 1820 Córdoba, under Juan Bautista Bustos, contested with Buenos Aires for control of the nation. The Federal Pact of 4 January 1831 began the Argentine Confederation.

eras.polity: Argentine Confederation, then the Argentine Republic
eras.note: The constitution was sanctioned on 1 May 1853, with Paraná as the Confederation's capital until 1861. After the Battle of Pavón (17 September 1861) the country was reunited as the Argentine Republic on 12 December 1861.

Argentine civil registration began with a national law of 1886 and the provinces started at different dates, most by 1900. Original books stay in the local civil registry office, with duplicates in the provincial or judicial archive; church records are the source for earlier years and still matter for marriages after 1886.

regions.label: Cuyo — Mendoza, San Juan, San Luis
regions.sub: Mendoza, San Juan, San Luis, San Rafael, Villa Mercedes

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Cuyo, under the Captaincy General of Chile
eras.note: Mendoza was founded in 1561 by Pedro del Castillo. Until 1776 Cuyo belonged to Chile, so colonial papers for Mendoza and San Juan can lie in Chilean as well as Argentine collections.

eras.polity: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata — Cuyo, then the Intendancy of Córdoba del Tucumán
eras.note: Mendoza and San Juan passed to the new viceroyalty in 1776. An intendancy of Cuyo with its capital at Mendoza was planned in 1782 and suppressed on 5 August 1783 in favour of the Intendancy of Córdoba del Tucumán, which governed Cuyo until 1813.

eras.polity: Province (Intendancy) of Cuyo — San Martín's base
eras.note: The Second Triumvirate created the Intendancy of Cuyo on 29 November 1813, capital Mendoza, with José de San Martín as its first governor. In 1817 he led the Army of the Andes across the cordillera into Chile. San Luis and San Juan separated on 1 March 1820, ending the province.

eras.polity: Provinces of Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis
eras.note: An earthquake in 1861 nearly destroyed Mendoza city, which was largely rebuilt. After the Battle of Pavón the provinces were part of the reunited Argentine Republic from 12 December 1861.

eras.polity: Argentine Republic — Mendoza, San Juan, San Luis
eras.note: Argentine civil registration dates from a national law of 1886, begun by each province at its own date, most by 1900. Wine-industry growth around 1900 drew tens of thousands of European immigrants, particularly Spaniards, to Mendoza.

regions.label: The North-West — Salta, Jujuy, Tucumán, Santiago del Estero, Catamarca, La Rioja
regions.sub: Salta, Jujuy, San Miguel de Tucumán, Santiago del Estero, Catamarca, La Rioja

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — the towns of Tucumán
eras.note: Juan Núñez de Prado received the territory of Tucumán in 1549 and founded Barco on the Dulce River. San Miguel de Tucumán was founded in 1565 and moved about 65 km in 1685 after Indigenous attacks; San Felipe de Lerma (Salta) was founded in 1582. The city before 1685 stood at an earlier site.

eras.polity: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata — Intendancy of Salta del Tucumán
eras.note: In 1783 the Tucumán intendancy was replaced by the Intendancy of Salta del Tucumán, and its capital moved from San Miguel de Tucumán to Salta. Tarija was added in 1807, so colonial papers for Salta can concern ground now in Bolivia.

eras.polity: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata — provinces carved from the intendancy
eras.note: Salta was freed from Spain at the Battle of Salta in 1813 and the province was created in 1814, then including Jujuy and parts of southern Bolivia and northern Chile. Independence was declared at Tucumán on 9 July 1816. Tucumán proclaimed a Federal Republic on 22 March 1820, from which Catamarca and Santiago del Estero withdrew in 1821. Bolivia annexed Tarija in 1826 and Jujuy left Salta in 1834.

eras.polity: Argentine Confederation, then the Argentine Republic
eras.note: The constitution was sanctioned on 1 May 1853. The provinces were part of the reunified Argentine Republic from 12 December 1861.

Argentine civil registration began with a national law of 1886 and the provinces started at different dates, most by 1900. Original books stay in the local civil registry office, with duplicates in the provincial or judicial archive; church records are the source for earlier years and still matter for marriages after 1886. Salta lost Yacuiba to Bolivia in 1900, and the National Government of Los Andes (1902) was returned to Salta as a department in 1943.

regions.label: Entre Ríos
regions.sub: Paraná, Concordia, Gualeguaychú, Gualeguay, Concepción del Uruguay

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Entre Ríos, settled from Santa Fe
eras.note: Spaniards first entered the area in 1520. Colonists from Santa Fe settled the Bajada del Paraná in the late 17th century. In 1783 Tomás de Rocamora gave many towns official status and was the first to call the region Entre Ríos. The Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata was created in 1776.

eras.polity: Province of Entre Ríos — the Republic of Entre Ríos 1820–21
eras.note: Francisco Ramírez declared the Republic of Entre Ríos on 29 September 1820; it ended with his death on 10 July 1821.

Paraná was the capital of the Confederation from 1853 to 1861, and the provincial capital moved to Concepción del Uruguay. Urquiza promoted colonisation by contract: Volga German, Russian (including Jewish and Polish), Italian, Swiss and French settlers.

eras.polity: Argentine Republic — Province of Entre Ríos
eras.note: Of 425,373 inhabitants in 1903, 153,067 were immigrants. Argentine civil registration began with a national law of 1886, and the provinces started at different dates.

regions.label: Corrientes and Misiones
regions.sub: Corrientes, Goya, Paso de los Libres, Posadas, Oberá

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Corrientes and the Jesuit reductions of the north
eras.note: Juan Torres de Vera y Aragón founded Corrientes on 3 April 1588. Jesuit mission towns were founded from 1609, the first of them San Ignacio in 1610, in the north of the province and in Misiones.

eras.polity: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (from 1776) — after the Jesuits
eras.note: Charles III expelled the Jesuits from the Spanish Americas in 1767, and the order itself was suppressed in 1773, after which the mission trade collapsed.

eras.polity: Province of Corrientes — Misiones contested with Paraguay
eras.note: Corrientes joined Artigas's Liga de los Pueblos Libres between 1814 and 1820. Corrientes forces took control of Misiones in 1830, Paraguay occupied it in 1838, and a Paraguayan attack on Corrientes in 1865 opened the Triple Alliance war.

eras.polity: Paraguayan War and the Misiones claim
eras.note: Paraguay's peace agreement with Argentina in 1876 gave up its claim to Misiones. The same year the Avellaneda immigration and colonisation law encouraged European settlement.

eras.polity: Province of Corrientes and National Territory of Misiones
eras.note: The national government created the National Territory of Misiones on 22 December 1881, detaching it from Corrientes, so Misiones records before that date may be filed under Corrientes. Argentine civil registration began with a national law of 1886, and the provinces started at different dates. Eldorado was founded in 1919.

eras.polity: Argentine Republic — provinces of Corrientes and Misiones
eras.note: Misiones became a province on 10 December 1953 under Law 14.294.

regions.label: Pampa and Patagonia — the southern frontier
regions.sub: Bahía Blanca, Santa Rosa, Neuquén, Trelew, Río Gallegos, Ushuaia

eras.note: In the 18th century the Crown founded coastal settlements at Carmen de Patagones, San José, Puerto Deseado and Nueva Colonia Floridablanca. The interior was not under Spanish settlement.

eras.polity: Argentine frontier — Indigenous lands to the south
eras.note: The interior south of the frontier was the land of Ranquel, Tehuelche, Pehuenche and Mapuche peoples. The Chubut area was disputed between Chile and Argentina until 1881.

eras.polity: Argentina — the Welsh colony in the Chubut valley
eras.note: 153 Welsh settlers arrived on the Mimosa on 28 July 1865 and walked to the Chubut valley; Argentina had offered land along the river. The Welsh Newspapers Online archive holds Y Drafod, and the National Library of Wales holds related material.

eras.polity: Argentina — the Conquest of the Desert
eras.note: Roca's campaigns began in late 1878, Villegas conquered Neuquén from 1881, and the last battle was on 18 October 1884, followed by a surrender in what is now Chubut. Many Indigenous people were killed or taken captive. The Chile–Argentina boundary treaty of 1881 recognised the Strait of Magellan as Chilean.

Argentina organised the National Territory of Chubut in 1884. Trelew was named for Lewis Jones when railway work began in 1886, with 465 further Welsh settlers arriving on the Vesta. Spanish- and Italian-born immigrants settled the lower Chubut valley between 1895 and 1915. Argentine civil registration began with a national law of 1886.
Chubut was declared a province in 1955.

regions.label: Norte Grande — Arica, Tarapacá, Antofagasta
regions.sub: Arica, Iquique, Pisagua, Antofagasta, Calama

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of Peru (Tarapacá); Audiencia of Charcas (Atacama)
eras.note: Tarapacá was administered by the Viceroyalty of Peru until 1824. Atacama was placed under the Audiencia of Charcas, though it is disputed whether that governed the coast.

eras.polity: Peru (Arica, Tarapacá) and Bolivia (the Litoral Department)
eras.note: Under Peru the area was part of the Department of Arequipa from 1821, the Department of Moquegua in 1857 and the Department of Tarapacá in 1877. The coast of Atacama was integrated into Bolivia as the Litoral Department, which Chile disputed. Events here before the war belong to Peruvian or Bolivian jurisdictions, not Chile's.

eras.polity: Chile — occupation in the War of the Pacific
eras.note: Chile occupied Antofagasta on 14 February 1879. The Treaty of Ancón, signed 20 October 1883, ceded Tarapacá to Chile and gave Chile temporary control of Arica and Tacna. Bolivia accepted Chilean administration of the Litoral in a truce in 1884.

eras.polity: Chile — nitrate ports; Arica under Chilean control
eras.note: The 1904 treaty between Chile and Bolivia set definite boundaries. The nitrate boom made Pisagua and Iquique major ports. The Santa María School massacre in Iquique took place in 1907.
The 1929 settlement between Chile and Peru gave Arica to Chile and Tacna to Peru. The present Tarapacá Region was created by Law 20,175 in 2007, separate from Arica and Parinacota.

regions.label: Central Chile — Santiago, Valparaíso, Coquimbo, Maule
regions.sub: Santiago, Valparaíso, La Serena, Copiapó, Talca

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Governorate of Chile (New Extremadura)
eras.note: Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago in 1541 and was named governor and captain general of New Extremadura. The Royal Audiencia of Santiago was founded in 1609.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Captaincy General of Chile, Intendancy of Santiago
eras.note: The intendancies of Santiago and Concepción were added in 1786. Sources date the status of captaincy general to 1778 or 1789 (contested), and Chile became administratively independent of the Viceroyalty of Peru in 1798.
A first government junta was formed on 18 September 1810. The Spanish reconquest followed the Battle of Rancagua on 2 October 1814, and independence as the Republic of Chile came on 12 February 1818.
Spain recognised Chile in 1844. Church records are the source for births, marriages and deaths before 1885.
Civil registration began in 1885. The records are kept in the local civil registration office of each municipality, with a duplicate in the Archivo General del Registro Civil in Santiago.

regions.label: Biobío and La Araucanía — the Frontier
regions.sub: Chillán, Concepción, Los Ángeles, Angol, Temuco

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — forts of Arauco and Tucapel
eras.note: The forts of San Felipe de Araucan and Tucapel were founded in 1553. The Battle of Curalaba on 23 December 1598 began the collapse of the southern Spanish cities.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — La Frontera on the Biobío
eras.note: The Biobío became the de facto frontier for the next century. The Parliament of Quillín in 1641 recognised Mapuche autonomy, so ground south of the river was not under Spanish civil administration.
The Intendancy of Concepción was created in 1786, one of two added that year with Santiago.

eras.polity: Republic of Chile — the Province of Arauco
eras.note: The Province of Arauco was created on 7 December 1852. By 1860 the land between the Biobío and the Malleco was mostly under Chilean control.

The occupation began in 1861 and ended with the re-founding of Villarrica on 1 January 1883. Mulchén grew from a fort built in 1861–62, and Temuco was founded in 1881. A Mapuche uprising on 12 November 1881 was defeated.

eras.polity: Republic of Chile — colonisation of the south
eras.note: The government encouraged European immigration after the occupation: 3,501 foreign settlers are recorded by 1886 and 5,657 arrived between 1883 and 1890. Mapuche communities were confined to about 3,000 reductions covering about 500,000 hectares.

regions.label: Valdivia, Osorno and Chiloé
regions.sub: Valdivia, Osorno, Puerto Montt, Ancud, Castro

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Valdivia and the southern cities
eras.note: Pedro de Valdivia founded Valdivia on 9 February 1552. Huilliche attacked the city on 24 November 1599, after the Battle of Curalaba.

eras.polity: Spanish retreat — Chiloé held; the Dutch at Valdivia
eras.note: Martín Ruiz de Gamboa conquered Chiloé in 1567 and settled Castro. Spanish forces left the Valdivia fort in 1604 and Dutch forces occupied the ruins in 1643.

eras.polity: Valdivia a fortified outpost; Chiloé a dependency of Peru
eras.note: Valdivia was refounded in 1645 and administered directly by the Viceroyalty of Peru until 1740. Chiloé became a direct dependency of the Viceroyalty of Peru in 1784. Ancud's founding as capital is dated 1767 or 1768 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Royalist south — Valdivia to 1820, Chiloé to 1826
eras.note: Cochrane's squadron captured Valdivia in 1820. Chiloé was a royalist stronghold from December 1817, and its last Spanish governor, Antonio de Quintanilla, surrendered on 15 January 1826.
Chiloé was incorporated into Chile after the surrender of January 1826.

The Law of Selective Immigration of 1845 aimed to bring settlers to the land between Valdivia and Puerto Montt. German immigration began in the mid-1840s, Carlos Anwandter arrived in 1850, and exiles of the 1848 revolutions settled mainly around Llanquihue.

regions.label: Aysén and Magallanes — Chilean Patagonia
regions.sub: Coyhaique, Punta Arenas, Puerto Natales, Porvenir

eras.note: Francisco de Ulloa reached the Taitao Peninsula in 1553, and Sarmiento de Gamboa's settlements date from 1579–1580.

eras.polity: Chile — the Strait of Magellan settlement
eras.note: The founding act at the Strait took place on 21 September 1843, and the settlement moved to Punta Arenas on 18 December 1848. It was used as a penal colony, with a prisoners' mutiny in December 1851. A census of 1854 counted 158 settlers; land grants from 1867 brought the first British immigrants.

eras.polity: Chile — Territory of Magellan; Aysén settled
eras.note: The boundary treaty of 1881 recognised the Strait as Chilean. Sheep farming boomed in the 1880s, and in 1906 Croatian immigrants overtook the British. The first Chilean colonisation attempt in Aysén settled about twenty Chiloé families at the Palena in 1888, and a 1902 arbitral award on the Argentine border opened the lands to exploitation.

eras.polity: Chile — Territory of Magellan; Aysén Territory then Province
eras.note: The Territory of Aysén was created on 30 December 1927 and became a province in 1929; Baquedano, now Coyhaique, was founded around then.
Decree Law 575 of 1974 made Aysén the XI Region. A 1994 arbitral award gave the Laguna del Desierto area to Argentina.

regions.label: Paraguay
regions.sub: Asunción, Concepción, Villarrica, Encarnación, Ciudad del Este

eras.note: Asunción was founded on 15 August 1537. Buenos Aires was abandoned in 1541 in favour of Asunción, and the first Jesuits arrived in 1588.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Paraguay and the Jesuit reductions
eras.note: Asunción became the centre of the Governorate of Guayrá in 1617. The Comunero Revolt ran from 1721 to 1735. San Ignacio Guazú, a mission town, was founded in 1609.

eras.polity: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (from 1776)
eras.note: Charles III expelled the Jesuits in 1767. With the creation of the viceroyalty in 1776 Paraguay became a provincial outpost of Buenos Aires.

A junta took power on 14–15 May 1811. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia became dictator in 1814 and died in 1840. Paraguay formally declared independence on 25 November 1842 and Carlos Antonio López became president in 1844.

eras.polity: Paraguay — the War of the Triple Alliance and occupation
eras.note: The war against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay began on 13 November 1864 and ended in 1870, with the death of Francisco Solano López at Cerro Corá on 1 March 1870. Foreign occupation ended in 1876. Argentina gained Misiones and land south of the Pilcomayo, and Brazil land north of the Apa. Loss of life was heavy and estimates range widely.

Civil registration began in 1880. The Dirección General del Registro del Estado Civil in Asunción is the main office; FamilySearch lists a civil registration collection for 1842–2012 whose coverage may vary. The Liberal Revolution of August 1904 began a period of Liberal rule.

eras.polity: Republic of Paraguay — the Chaco War and after
eras.note: The Chaco War with Bolivia ran from 1932 to 1935, and the peace treaty was signed on 21 July 1938. Alfredo Stroessner seized power in 1954; he was overthrown in 1989.

regions.label: Piedmont — Savoy, Turin and the Po plain
regions.sub: Torino, Cuneo, Asti, Alessandria, Novara, Vercelli, Biella, Domodossola

eras.note: The Dukes of Savoy moved their capital from Chambéry to Turin in 1562 (1563 in some accounts). Much of the east of today's Piedmont lay outside the duchy: half of Montferrat belonged to the Gonzaga of Mantua until 1708, and parts of the Duchy of Milan passed to Savoy under the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.

Savoy received Sicily in 1713 and exchanged it for Sardinia in 1720, after which the state was the Kingdom of Sardinia although its centre remained Turin. Novara and Tortona, with the Langhe, passed to Charles Emmanuel III in the peace that closed the War of the Polish Succession (1738).
The Sub-Alpine Republic was set up in June 1800 and came under full French control in 1801.

France annexed Piedmont in September 1802. French-style civil-status registers for Piedmont are dated about 1802 or 1804 to 1814, and FamilySearch lists Turin State Archive civil registration for 1802-1816.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sardinia — restored 1814; Genoa added 1815
eras.note: The kingdom was restored after Napoleon and gained the Republic of Genoa at the Congress of Vienna. The Statuto Albertino constitution dates from 1847-48, and Savoy and Nice were ceded to France in 1860. Civil-status registers under the Sardinian system are generally dated from 1839; the Italian state registers start in 1866.

eras.polity: Kingdom, then Republic of Italy — Piedmont
eras.note: The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861 with Turin as its first capital, which it remained until 1865. Italian civil registration began in 1866 for most of northern and central Italy.

regions.label: Aosta Valley — Savoy's French-speaking valley
regions.sub: Aosta, Courmayeur, Châtillon, Pont-Saint-Martin, Cogne

eras.polity: County of Aosta under the House of Savoy
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Savoy, then the Kingdom of Sardinia
eras.note: Modern French became the sole official language of the valley in 1536, and French armies occupied it in 1539-1563, 1691 and 1704-1706. Its autonomy rights were revoked in 1770.

eras.polity: France — arrondissement of Aoste, Doire department
eras.note: The valley was ruled by the First French Empire as an arrondissement of the department of Doire.
Restored to the Kingdom of Sardinia after the Napoleonic period.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Italy — part of Turin province, then its own province of Aosta
eras.note: The valley was incorporated into the province of Turin in 1861. The province of Aosta was created in 1927 and dissolved in 1945, and Italian civil registration began in 1866 for most of northern Italy.

eras.polity: Italy — autonomous region of Valle d'Aosta
eras.note: Italian and French were made official languages in 1946 and the region received special autonomous status in 1948.

regions.label: Liguria — the Genoese Riviera
regions.sub: Genova, Savona, Imperia, Sanremo, La Spezia, Sarzana

eras.note: Genoa was governed by a doge, and after the reform of 1528 doges served two-year terms. Corsica was ceded to France in 1768.
Napoleon replaced the Republic of Genoa with the Ligurian Republic in June 1797. It had a first constitution in December 1797 and a second in 1802, and Austrian forces held it briefly in 1800.

eras.polity: Annexed to France — departments of Apennins, Gênes and Montenotte
eras.note: France annexed the territory in June 1805 as the departments of Apennins, Gênes and Montenotte.

eras.polity: Republic of Genoa restored for a few months
eras.note: The republic was restored from 28 April to 28 July 1814, and was annexed to Piedmont-Sardinia on 3 January 1815 as the Duchy of Genoa.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sardinia — Duchy of Genoa
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna gave the former republic to the Kingdom of Sardinia, which became the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

eras.polity: Kingdom, then Republic of Italy — Liguria
eras.note: Italian civil registration began in 1866 for most of northern Italy; the Antenati portal carries registers from the La Spezia and Genoa State Archives.

regions.label: Lombardy — the Duchy of Milan, Pavia and Valtellina
regions.sub: Milano, Pavia, Como, Varese, Lecco, Lodi, Cremona, Sondrio, Bormio

eras.polity: Duchy of Milan — Spanish Habsburg rule
eras.note: Habsburg rule began in 1535 when the last Sforza duke died, Spain governed from 1556, and Philip II's possession was recognised in 1559. Valtellina, in the north-east, was not part of the duchy: it was ruled by the Three Leagues (Grisons) from 1512 to 1797.

eras.polity: Duchy of Milan — Austrian Habsburg rule
eras.note: Austria took over in 1707 and the Treaty of Baden (1714) confirmed it. The 1743 Treaty of Worms promised part of the Duchy of Pavia to the King of Sardinia, so the Pavia area is the one to check when a family appears in Milanese and in Savoyard records.

eras.polity: French conquest, Cisalpine Republic, then Italian Republic
eras.note: Napoleon's forces took the duchy in 1796 and Valtellina joined the Cisalpine Republic in October 1797 (10 or 22 October depending on the source). Austria occupied the Cisalpine Republic in April 1799 and France restored it in June 1800.

The kingdom was proclaimed on 17 March 1805 and ended with Napoleon's abdication on 11 April 1814. Civil-status registers for Lombardy and the Veneto from this period are generally dated 1806 to 1814 or 1815.

eras.polity: Austrian Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia — capital Milan
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna created the kingdom on 9 June 1815, with Milan as capital until 1859. After 1815 parish priests again kept the civil-status registers, with a duplicate copy sent to the tribunal.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sardinia — Lombardy ceded by Austria
eras.note: Austria ceded Lombardy up to the Mincio under the Treaty of Zurich after the defeat at Solferino in 1859, and it was passed to Sardinia-Piedmont.

eras.polity: Kingdom, then Republic of Italy — Lombardy
eras.note: Italian civil registration began in 1866 for most of northern Italy, and some sources date the end of the parish-priest registers in Lombardy to 1860 rather than 1866.

regions.label: Bergamo, Brescia and Mantua — Venetian and Gonzaga Lombardy
regions.sub: Bergamo, Brescia, Mantova, Salò, Desenzano, Edolo

eras.polity: Republic of Venice (Brescia, Bergamo); Gonzaga duchy of Mantua
eras.note: Brescia was sold to Venice in 1426 and Bergamo passed from Milan to Venice in 1428, so their records are not Milanese. Mantua was raised to a duchy in 1530 under the Gonzaga, whose rule ended in 1708.

eras.polity: Republic of Venice (Brescia, Bergamo); Habsburg Mantua
eras.note: The Habsburgs took Mantua in 1708. Joseph II united Mantua with the Duchy of Milan on 26 September 1786 and Leopold II restored its separate administration on 24 January 1791.
Mantua fell to the French in 1797 and the Treaty of Campo Formio (17 October 1797) recognised the inclusion of Bergamo and other territories in the Cisalpine Republic.
Part of the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy, proclaimed on 17 March 1805. Civil-status registers for Lombardy and the Veneto of this period are generally dated 1806 to 1814 or 1815.
Brescia and Bergamo were assigned to Lombardy–Venetia in 1815. Brescia's population overthrew the Austrian administration in March 1849 in the Ten Days of Brescia.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sardinia — Bergamo and Brescia; Mantua still Austrian
eras.note: Austria ceded Lombardy only up to the Mincio and kept the fortresses of Mantua and Peschiera, so Mantua stayed under Austria in 1859.

Mantua was not Italian until Austria lost Venetia in 1866, when it was transferred through France to Italy (19 October 1866, with a plebiscite on 21-22 October). Italian civil registration began in 1866 for most of northern Italy.

regions.label: Parma, Piacenza, Reggio and Modena — the duchies
regions.sub: Parma, Piacenza, Reggio nell'Emilia, Modena, Guastalla, Mirandola

eras.polity: Duchies of Parma and Piacenza (Farnese, from 1545) and of Modena and Reggio (Este)
eras.note: Pope Paul III created the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza in 1545 and the Farnese line died out in 1731. Modena and Reggio were an Este duchy from 1452; the Este kept them after the papacy seized Ferrara in 1597. Parma passed to the Habsburgs under the 1738 treaty and returned to the Bourbons in 1748 with Guastalla added, after the Gonzaga there died out in 1746.

eras.polity: French occupation, Cispadane and Cisalpine Republics, Kingdom of Italy
eras.note: The French occupied Modena in 1796 and created the Cispadane Republic. Parma was ceded to France in 1801 and formally annexed in 1808. Napoleonic civil-status registers run from 1806 for Modena and Parma.

eras.polity: Restored duchies — Parma under Marie-Louise, then Bourbon-Parma; Modena under the Este-Habsburg dukes
eras.note: Parma was given to Marie-Louise in April 1814 (she ruled until 1847) and then to the Bourbon-Parma dukes, and Guastalla was ceded to Modena after 1847. Francis IV ruled Modena from 1814 and added Massa and Carrara in 1829; the dukes were briefly ousted in 1831 and 1848. Antenati holds Parma civil-status files for 1806-1865 and Modena's Austro-Estense civil-status series dated 1852-1865.

eras.polity: United Provinces of Central Italy, annexed to Sardinia
eras.note: In December 1859 Parma and Modena joined Tuscany in the United Provinces of Central Italy, which were annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia in March 1860.
Italian civil registration began in 1866 for most of northern and central Italy.

regions.label: Bologna, Ferrara and Romagna — the Papal Legations
regions.sub: Bologna, Ferrara, Ravenna, Forlì, Cesena, Rimini, Imola

eras.polity: Papal States — Bologna from 1506, Ferrara from 1597, the Romagna legations
eras.note: Pope Julius II entered Bologna on 10 November 1506 and the Papal States annexed the Duchy of Ferrara in 1597. The four northern papal areas, Bologna, Ferrara, Forlì and Ravenna, were governed by cardinal legates and were called the Legations.

eras.polity: French conquest, Cispadane and Cisalpine Republics, Kingdom of Italy
eras.note: Napoleon entered Bologna on 19 June 1796, the Cispadane Republic was formed at the Congress of Reggio (27 December 1796 - 9 January 1797) and the Cisalpine Republic succeeded it on 9 July 1797. Civil-status registers of the former Papal lands in this period are generally dated 1810 to 1814, and from 1806 where the territory was in the Kingdom of Italy.

eras.polity: Papal States restored — Legations of Bologna, Ferrara and the Romagne
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna restored the Legations to the Pope. A motu proprio of 6 July 1816 made Bologna, Ferrara, Forlì and Ravenna the first-class delegations (Forlì included Cesena and Rimini; Ravenna included Faenza and Imola), and in 1850 they were regrouped as legations. A part of upper Romagna in the Apennines belonged to Tuscany until the 1920s.

eras.polity: United Provinces of Central Italy, annexed to Sardinia
eras.note: After the 1859 war the Legations became part of the United Provinces of Central Italy, and Bologna voted for union on 11-12 March 1860.
Italian civil registration began in 1866 for most of northern and central Italy.

regions.label: South Tyrol (Alto Adige) — Habsburg Tyrol until 1919
regions.sub: Bolzano, Merano, Bressanone, Brunico, Vipiteno, Silandro

eras.polity: County of Tyrol with the prince-bishoprics of Brixen and Trent
eras.note: Much of the land was held by the prince-bishops of Trent and Brixen. The earliest surviving Catholic parish register of the diocese of Bozen-Brixen, from Stilfes, begins in 1565.

eras.polity: Split between Bavaria and the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy
eras.note: Austria ceded northern Tyrol to Bavaria after Napoleon's victory in 1805, and the Kingdom of Italy took southern Tyrol in 1810. The Congress of Vienna returned the whole of Tyrol to Austria.

eras.polity: Austrian Tyrol — from 1867 a crown land of Cisleithania
eras.note: About 89 percent of the population spoke German in the 1910 census. The Catholic parish registers served as the official civil registers until the end of 1923.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Italy — province of Bolzano
eras.note: Italy occupied the area in November 1918 and the Treaty of Saint-Germain gave it the territory south of the Alpine watershed; the annexation is dated 1919 or October 1920 depending on the source, and the present province was formed in 1926. Italian state civil registers replaced the parish registers on 1 January 1924, and the 1939 Option Agreement let German speakers emigrate to Germany or stay.

eras.polity: German occupation — de facto annexed to Greater Germany
eras.note: After Italy's surrender in 1943 German forces occupied the region.

The Gruber-De Gasperi Agreement of September 1946 created the autonomous region of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol and the autonomy statute followed in 1972. The South Tyrol Provincial Archive has placed the Catholic parish registers of the diocese of Bozen-Brixen online, covering the beginnings to 31 December 1923.

regions.label: Northern Tuscany — Florence, Pisa, Lucca, Arezzo
regions.sub: Florence, Pisa, Lucca, Livorno, Pistoia, Prato, Arezzo

eras.note: Before registers. The Florentine Republic fell after the siege of 1529-30; Charles V made the Medici hereditary rulers on 12 August 1530.

eras.polity: Duchy of Florence, from 1569 the Grand Duchy of Tuscany (Habsburg-Lorraine from 1737)
eras.note: A constitution of 27 April 1532 created the hereditary duchy, and Pius V made Cosimo I Grand Duke on 27 August 1569. Parish baptism and marriage registers begin in 1563 and burials in 1614. Lucca was a separate state throughout, as the Republic of Lucca, and was not absorbed by Tuscany until 1847.
The Treaty of Aranjuez of 21 March 1801 replaced the grand duchy with the Kingdom of Etruria, which was annexed to France on 30 May 1808.

eras.polity: French Empire — the Departments of Tuscany
eras.note: Elisa Bonaparte headed a General Government of the Departments of Tuscany from March 1809. Antenati lists the Napoleonic civil registers for Tuscany as 1808-1814.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Tuscany restored; Duchy of Lucca (Bourbon-Parma) 1815-1847
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna made Lucca a separate duchy, which Leopold II absorbed in October 1847. A provisional government took over in 1859, and Tuscany was annexed to Sardinia on 22 March 1860 after a referendum. Antenati lists the Tuscan pre-unification civil series as 1815-1865.
Italian state civil registration is dated 1866 by FamilySearch, while Antenati's Tuscan listing dates the Italian series from 1860, so the start year depends on the comune.

regions.label: Southern Tuscany — Siena, Grosseto and the Maremma
regions.sub: Siena, Grosseto, Montepulciano, Orbetello, Piombino, Elba

eras.note: Before registers. Cosimo I de' Medici conquered the Republic of Siena in 1555.

eras.polity: Duchy and Grand Duchy of Tuscany; the Presidi coast held separately
eras.note: Spain kept the former Sienese coastal fortresses of Porto Ercole, Orbetello and Talamone, with Porto Longone on Elba, as the State of the Presidi from 1557. It was Spanish to 1707, Austrian from 1708, and from the Treaty of Vienna of 1738 a dependency of the Kingdom of Naples, so those towns were not Tuscan before 1801.
Naples ceded the Presidi to France in 1801, and France handed them to the new Kingdom of Etruria.

eras.polity: French Empire — the Departments of Tuscany
eras.note: Antenati lists the Napoleonic civil registers for Tuscany as 1808-1814.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Tuscany restored, with the Presidi and Piombino
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna gave the restored grand duchy the State of the Presidi and the Principality of Piombino. Tuscany was annexed to Sardinia on 22 March 1860.

eras.polity: Italy — Provinces of Siena and Grosseto

regions.label: Umbria — Perugia, Terni, Spoleto
regions.sub: Perugia, Terni, Spoleto, Foligno, Assisi, Orvieto, Gubbio

eras.polity: Free comuni and signorie (Perugia, Foligno, Città di Castello)
eras.note: Before registers. Local families took power in the early 14th century: the Vitelli in Città di Castello, the Baglioni in Perugia and the Trinci in Foligno.
Cardinal Albornoz had brought the region under the Papal States by the middle of the 14th century, and the papacy ruled it without challenge until the end of the 18th century.
Declared in February 1798; Neapolitan troops ended it in October 1799.
The remaining Papal States were annexed to the French Empire on 17 May 1809. FamilySearch dates the Napoleonic civil registers of the former Papal States to 1810-1815; other summaries give 1810-1814.

The Congress of Vienna restored papal rule in 1814-15, and the pope held Umbria until 1860. Civil registration was dropped after the French and resumed with the Italian state in 1866, so these decades rest on parish registers.
Piedmont annexed Umbria, with the Marche, in 1860, and the region joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

eras.polity: Italy — Provinces of Perugia and Terni
eras.note: Rieti was detached from Umbria and added to Lazio in 1923, and Umbria was divided into the provinces of Perugia and Terni in 1927.

regions.label: The Marche — Ancona, Urbino, Macerata, Ascoli
regions.sub: Ancona, Pesaro, Urbino, Macerata, Fermo, Ascoli Piceno

eras.polity: Marches of Ancona, Camerino and Fermo; Duchy of Urbino
eras.note: Nominally Papal, but local lords (among them the Malatesta of Rimini and the Montefeltro of Urbino) and free communes held most of the land, and Ancona was a maritime republic in the 12th century. The Duchy of Urbino was dissolved in 1631.
From 1631 the Marche was firmly part of the Papal States.

eras.polity: Republic of Ancona (1797-98), then the Roman Republic (1798-99)
eras.note: The Roman Republic was declared in February 1798 and ended in October 1799 when Neapolitan troops restored papal rule.

Napoleon annexed the Marches (Urbino, Ancona, Macerata, Camerino) to the Kingdom of Italy on 2 April 1808. FamilySearch dates the Napoleonic civil registers of the former Papal States to 1810-1815; other summaries give 1810-1814.
Joachim Murat briefly occupied the region in 1815. Civil registration was dropped after the French and resumed with the Italian state in 1866, so these decades rest on parish registers.

The Marche was annexed to the Kingdom of Italy by plebiscite on 4 November 1860. Seven Montefeltro municipalities moved from the Province of Pesaro and Urbino to the Province of Rimini, in Emilia-Romagna, on 15 August 2009.

regions.label: Abruzzo and Molise
regions.sub: L'Aquila, Chieti, Pescara, Teramo, Campobasso, Isernia, Termoli

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sicily under Frederick II, then the Angevin Kingdom of Naples
eras.note: Before registers. Frederick II set up Abruzzo as a justiciarate in the 1230s, and in 1273 Charles I of Anjou divided it at the Pescara river into Abruzzo Citeriore and Ulteriore.
Alfonso V of Aragon took the Kingdom of Naples in 1442; the Abruzzo source dates his conquest 1443. L'Aquila lost political and economic weight to Chieti under the Aragonese.
Spanish control is dated 1503 or 1504 depending on the source. The Apennine earthquakes of 1703 devastated L'Aquila, and an earthquake in 1706 hit Sulmona.
The Treaty of Rastatt gave Naples to Charles VI in 1714. A Spanish army took Naples in 1734 and Charles of Bourbon was installed as king in 1735.

eras.polity: Napoleonic Kingdom of Naples (Joseph Bonaparte, then Murat)
eras.note: Napoleonic civil registration was introduced to the Kingdom of Naples in January 1809 under Murat. In 1806 Abruzzo Ultra was split into Ultra I and Ultra II at the Gran Sasso, and Molise's provincial borders were largely set by 1811.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Naples; from 8 December 1816 the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
eras.note: Civil registration was reintroduced in 1816, and from then to 1865 the birth and marriage acts of the south carry church baptism or marriage details. Abruzzo passed to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860 and to the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

eras.polity: Italy — the region of Abruzzi e Molise
eras.note: Abruzzo and Molise formed one region, Abruzzi e Molise, until they were separated in 1963.

eras.polity: Italy — Abruzzo and Molise, separate regions

regions.label: Apulia — Bari, Foggia and Salento
regions.sub: Bari, Foggia, Lecce, Taranto, Brindisi, Otranto, Barletta

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sicily, from 1282 the Kingdom of Naples
eras.note: Before registers. Frederick II made Foggia one of his residences, and after 1282 the mainland, Apulia included, came under the Kingdom of Naples.
Alfonso V of Aragon conquered Naples in 1442 and united it with Sicily under Aragonese rule.
The Treaty of Rastatt gave Naples to Charles VI in 1714.
A Spanish army conquered Naples and Sicily in 1734, and Charles of Bourbon was installed as king in 1735.

An act of 8 August 1806 reorganised the kingdom on the French model. Terra d'Otranto, seat Lecce, covered Salento and today's Taranto and Brindisi provinces (without Fasano and Cisternino, which belonged to Bari).
The Restoration civil registers of the south, also called Bourbon registers, run from 1816 to 1865. Terra d'Otranto's administrative organisation was finalised from 1 January 1817.

eras.polity: Italy — Provinces of Foggia, Bari and Lecce
eras.note: Apulia was incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy in 1861 as the provinces of Foggia, Bari and Lecce, and Terra d'Otranto became the Province of Lecce. Brigandage followed unification.

eras.polity: Italy — Provinces of Foggia, Bari, Lecce, Taranto and Brindisi
eras.note: The Ionian province (Taranto) was created in 1923 and the Province of Brindisi in 1927, both cut from Terra d'Otranto; Fasano and Cisternino passed from Bari to Brindisi. A 19th-century record for a Taranto or Brindisi town may be filed under Lecce.

regions.label: Basilicata — Potenza and Matera
regions.sub: Potenza, Matera, Melfi, Lagonegro, Maratea, Policoro

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sicily (Hohenstaufen), then the Angevins
eras.note: Before registers. Frederick II created the Justiciarate of Basilicata, and the Angevins replaced the Swabians in the 13th century.
Alfonso V of Aragon conquered Naples in 1442.
In 1663 a new province was created with Matera as its capital; until then Matera had belonged to Terra d'Otranto.
The Treaty of Rastatt gave Naples to Charles VI in 1714.
The Bourbons took control in 1735.
Napoleonic civil registers in the Kingdom of Naples are dated 1809 or 1810-1814 depending on the source.
The 1857 earthquake devastated much of the region. On 18 August 1860 the Potenza insurrection led Basilicata to declare its annexation to the Kingdom of Italy.

eras.polity: Italy — Provinces of Potenza and Matera
eras.note: Brigandage followed unification. The population fell from 539,258 in 1881 to 485,911 in 1911, mainly through emigration overseas.

regions.label: Sardinia
regions.sub: Cagliari, Sassari, Nuoro, Oristano, Alghero, Olbia

eras.polity: Pisan territories, Doria and Malaspina lordships, and the Judicate of Arborea
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon — Kingdom of Sardinia
eras.note: James II of Aragon took the Pisan territories in 1323-24. Alfonso V bought the remaining Arborean territories in 1420, ending the judicates, and the kingdom was incorporated into the Crown of Aragon in 1460.
Parish baptism and marriage registers begin in 1563 and burials in 1614. Entries before the mid-18th century are mostly in Latin or Spanish, and Italian generally begins in the 1760s.
The island became Habsburg territory in 1708, and the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) assigned it to Charles VI.
Spain reconquered the island in 1717. The Treaty of The Hague of 17 February 1720 gave it to Victor Amadeus II of Savoy in exchange for Sicily.

Napoleon never ruled the island, so Napoleonic civil registers do not apply to it. The Savoy court sat at Cagliari from 1798 to 1814 after the French took Piedmont, and the 'Perfect Fusion' of 1847 (some sources say 1848) centralised the Savoyard states in Turin.
The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861 by the Sardinian Parliament. The state civil registers held at Cagliari begin in 1866, although one genealogy site gives 1861.

regions.label: Western and central Sicily — Palermo, Trapani, Agrigento
regions.sub: Palermo, Trapani, Marsala, Agrigento, Caltanissetta, Enna, Cefalù

eras.note: Before registers. Roger II was proclaimed king in 1130, and the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 ended Angevin rule on the island.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sicily, separate from the mainland
eras.note: The Peace of Caltabellotta (1302) formalised the split between the island and the mainland kingdom of Naples.

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon — Kingdom of Sicily
eras.note: The Compromise of Caspe of 1412 added Sicily permanently to the Crown of Aragon.
Spanish domination is dated 1479 to 1713.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sicily under Victor Amadeus II of Savoy
eras.note: The Treaty of Utrecht gave Sicily to the House of Savoy in 1713.
Austria took Sicily in 1720 in exchange for Sardinia (Treaty of The Hague).
Bourbon rule began with the conquest of 1735. Britain occupied Sicily from 1806 to 1814, and a British-style constitution was issued in 1812.

The island kingdom merged with Naples into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1816. Civil registration on Sicily began in 1820, eleven years after the mainland. Garibaldi landed at Marsala on 11 May 1860 and took Palermo between 27 May and 6 June.
Plebiscites brought Sicily into Piedmont-Sardinia, and the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861.

regions.label: Ingria — Saint Petersburg and the Neva
regions.sub: Saint Petersburg, Gatchina, Kronstadt, Luga, Tikhvin

eras.polity: Novgorod Republic — Novgorod Land reached the Gulf of Finland
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Grand Principality of Moscow, from 1547 the Tsardom of Russia
eras.note: Ivan III annexed Novgorod and its lands in 1478 and took four-fifths of its land. The central Muscovite records of the period, such as the diplomatic and service-rank fonds, are in RGADA, Moscow.

The Treaty of Stolbovo gave Ingria to Sweden in 1617. The end date is contested: Saint Petersburg was founded in 1703 during the Russian reconquest, but the Treaty of Nystad ceded Ingria formally only in 1721.

eras.polity: Russian Empire — Ingermanland, from 1710 Saint Petersburg Governorate
eras.note: Ingermanland became a governorate in 1706 or 1708 (the sources differ) and was renamed Saint Petersburg Governorate on 3 June 1710; it became Petrograd Governorate on 18 August 1914. Gatchina, Kronstadt, Narva, Oranienbaum and Pavlovsk were 'supernumerary towns' outside the uyezds, and the Vyborg and Kexholm lands were merged into a separate Governorate of Vyborg after 1743, so Vyborg is not under this governorate.

eras.polity: Petrograd, Leningrad Governorate (1924), Leningrad Oblast (from 1 August 1927)
eras.note: Civil registration offices (ZAGS) replaced parish registers in 1918. Ingrian Finns were deported from the late 1920s (about 18,000 from North Ingria in 1929-1931, about 7,000 in 1935, about 20,000 from the border parishes in 1936), and Lutheran churches and Finnish schools were closed in 1937. The Siege of Leningrad lasted from 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Saint Petersburg and Leningrad Oblast
eras.note: After a 1991 referendum the city of Leningrad took back the name Saint Petersburg; the surrounding oblast kept the name Leningrad Oblast, so the city and the oblast are filed separately.

regions.label: Olonets and Karelia — Petrozavodsk, Onega and the White Sea coast
regions.sub: Petrozavodsk, Olonets, Lodeynoye Pole, Povenets, Kem, Pudozh

eras.note: Before registers. Karelians were converted to Orthodoxy in 1227 and Karelia became part of Novgorod in the thirteenth century.

eras.polity: Muscovy and the Russian Empire — before the Olonets Governorate
eras.note: Ivan III annexed the area with Novgorod in the later fifteenth century. Peter the Great began ironworks near Petrozavodsk in 1701-1714; there was no Olonets Governorate until 1801.

Created 21 September 1801 with seven uyezd towns: Petrozavodsk, Kargopol, Lodeynoye Pole, Olonets, Povenets, Pudozh and Vytegra. Kemsky Uyezd on the White Sea coast stayed in Arkhangelsk Governorate, and Kargopol, an Olonets seat, lies in the neighbouring Russian North region of this map, so a family can be filed under either governorate.

eras.polity: Karelian Labour Commune (8 June 1920), Karelian ASSR (1923); Karelo-Finnish SSR from 1940
eras.note: The Olonets Governorate was abolished in 1922. The Karelian ASSR was created in 1923, and Karelia became the Karelo-Finnish SSR in 1940. Sandarmokh in Karelia is one of the largest burial sites of the 1937 executions.
The Finnish army crossed the border on 1 July 1941 and left Petrozavodsk on 27 June 1944.

eras.polity: Karelo-Finnish SSR, from 1956 the Karelian ASSR
eras.note: The Karelo-Finnish SSR was reduced to an autonomous republic within the RSFSR in 1956.
The Karelian ASSR declared sovereignty in August 1990 and was renamed the Republic of Karelia in 1991.

regions.label: The Kola Peninsula — Murmansk and the Tersky coast
regions.sub: Murmansk, Kola, Kandalaksha, Kuzomen, Umba

eras.polity: Sámi lands and the Russian White Sea coast
eras.note: Before registers. The Sámi are the region's indigenous people, and Russians began exploring the White Sea shores in the twelfth century.

eras.polity: Arkhangelsk Viceroyalty (26 March 1784), Arkhangelsk Governorate from 1796 — Kolsky Uyezd
eras.note: Kola was the centre of Kolsky Uyezd and was destroyed in the Crimean War in 1854. Murmansk was founded only in 1916, so everything earlier is filed under Kola or the Arkhangelsk Governorate.

eras.polity: Murmansk Okrug in Leningrad Oblast; Kandalaksha district in the Karelian ASSR
eras.note: The Treaty of Tartu ceded the Pechenga (Petsamo) area to Finland in 1920. Before 1938 the peninsula was split between Murmansk Okrug of Leningrad Oblast and the Kandalaksha district of the Karelian ASSR.
Murmansk Oblast was created on 28 May 1938 from Murmansk Okrug and the Kandalaksha district. Pechenga returned to the RSFSR in 1940 according to one source (other accounts give 1944).

regions.label: The Russian North — Arkhangelsk, Vologda and the Dvina
regions.sub: Arkhangelsk, Vologda, Veliky Ustyug, Kargopol, Mezen, Totma

eras.note: Before registers. The Dvina lands were Novgorod's fur territory; Moscow annexed them in 1397 and Novgorod recovered them in 1398.

eras.polity: Grand Principality of Moscow, from 1547 the Tsardom of Russia
eras.note: Vologda passed to Moscow with the annexation of Novgorod. The central Muscovite records of the period, such as the diplomatic and service-rank fonds, are in RGADA, Moscow.
Peter the Great created Archangelgorod Governorate in 1708 as one of the first eight governorates; it was abolished in 1780. The Holy Synod required Orthodox metrical books from the 1720s.

eras.polity: Vologda Viceroyalty (1780) and Arkhangelsk Viceroyalty (26 March 1784)
eras.note: The old governorate became the Vologda Viceroyalty in 1780, and Arkhangelsk was split off as its own viceroyalty on 26 March 1784. Mezen and Pinega became uyezd towns in 1780.

Arkhangelsk Governorate dates from 12 December 1796. Vologda had ten uyezds, among them Veliky Ustyug, Totma, Solvychegodsk, Velsk and Yarensk. Complete 1897 census returns are known to survive for Arkhangelsk Governorate, one of only two governorates (with Tobolsk) where complete returns remain.
Northern Krai merged the Vologda, Arkhangelsk and Northern Dvina governorates and the Komi-Zyryan Autonomous Oblast, with its centre at Arkhangelsk.

regions.label: Novgorod and Pskov
regions.sub: Veliky Novgorod, Pskov, Staraya Russa, Borovichi, Velikiye Luki

eras.polity: Novgorod Republic, and the Pskov Republic after 1348
eras.note: Before registers. Pskov became formally independent of Novgorod in 1348 (the date of the Treaty of Bolotovo is debated), but the archbishop of Novgorod kept the title 'of Novgorod the Great and Pskov' until 1589.

eras.polity: Grand Principality of Moscow, from 1547 the Tsardom of Russia
eras.note: Novgorod was annexed in 1478: the veche was abolished and four-fifths of the land was taken. Pskov was annexed on 13 January 1510 and about 300 families were deported and replaced with loyalists, which breaks family continuity in both cities.
Sweden occupied Novgorod on 17 July 1611 during the Ingrian War, which ended with the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617.

eras.polity: Tsardom of Russia, from 1708 within Ingermanland (Saint Petersburg) Governorate
eras.note: In the 1708 reform the Novgorod area was part of Ingermanland Governorate, renamed Saint Petersburg Governorate in 1710.

A separate Novgorod Governorate of five provinces was created in 1727, and in 1772 Velikiye Luki Province moved to the new Pskov Governorate (seat Opochka). Both became viceroyalties in 1775 and 1777 and governorates again in 1796. Orthodox parish books were kept in duplicate, a church set and a consistory set.
Both governorates were abolished on 1 August 1927. Pechory, Izborsk, Vyshgorodok and Pytalovo went to Estonia and Latvia in 1920 and returned to Pskov Oblast in 1945.
German troops occupied western parts of the present Novgorod Oblast, including the city of Novgorod, and the Pskov area.

eras.polity: Novgorod Oblast (5 July 1944), Velikiye Luki Oblast (22 August 1944), Pskov Oblast (23 August 1944)
eras.note: Velikiye Luki Oblast was created one day before Pskov Oblast, so Velikiye Luki records of the period are under a third oblast.

regions.label: Tver — Rzhev, Torzhok, Kashin and Bezhetsk
regions.sub: Tver, Rzhev, Torzhok, Kashin, Bezhetsk, Ostashkov

eras.note: Before registers. Tver competed with Moscow for supremacy until 1485.

eras.polity: Grand Principality of Moscow, from 1547 the Tsardom of Russia
eras.note: The Principality of Tver ended in 1485 when Moscow absorbed it. The central Muscovite records of the period are in RGADA, Moscow.

eras.polity: Tver Viceroyalty (25 November 1775), Tver Governorate (12 December 1796 to 12 August 1929)
eras.note: The governorate's area is now divided between Tver and Moscow oblasts, with minor parts in Yaroslavl and Novgorod oblasts, so some Tver Governorate families sit under a neighbouring modern oblast.

eras.polity: Central Industrial Oblast (14 January 1929), Moscow Oblast (3 June 1929)
eras.note: The Central Industrial Oblast included the former Moscow, Ryazan, Tver, Tula, Vladimir and Kaluga governorates and was renamed Moscow Oblast on 3 June 1929.

Kalinin Oblast was formed on 29 January 1935 from parts of the Western, Leningrad and Moscow oblasts. In 1940 Polish prisoners from the NKVD camp at Ostashkov were shot in Kalinin and buried at Mednoye, part of the Katyn massacre.

eras.polity: German occupation of part of the oblast
eras.note: German troops occupied part of the oblast from 1941 to 1943.
Kalinin Oblast was renamed Tver Oblast on 17 July 1990.

regions.label: Moscow and its governorate
regions.sub: Moscow, Mozhaisk, Volokolamsk, Dmitrov, Klin, Podolsk

eras.note: Moscow annexed Novgorod in 1478, Tver in 1485, Pskov in 1510 and Ryazan in 1521. The central Muscovite records are in RGADA.

Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547. In the Time of Troubles (1598-1613) Polish forces held Moscow's Kremlin until the garrison surrendered on 27 October 1612, and Michael Romanov was elected tsar on 21 February 1613.

Moscow Governorate was created on 29 December 1708 (18 December Old Style) and had 13 uyezds. Orthodox metrical books (births, marriages, deaths) were required from the 1720s and kept in duplicate, one set in the church and one in the consistory; a large part of the church copies is held today in district civil registration offices.

eras.polity: Soviet Russia — Moscow Governorate until 14 January 1929
eras.note: Civil registration offices (ZAGS) replaced parish registers in 1918; registers from before 1918 are open to all, later civil-status records only to relatives.

Twenty-six districts passed to Kalinin Oblast in January 1935 and 77 were separated to form Tula and Ryazan oblasts in September 1937. In 1944 further districts went to Kaluga and Vladimir oblasts, so a village's oblast can change between records.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Moscow a federal city, separate from Moscow Oblast
eras.note: The city of Moscow is a federal city of its own and is not part of Moscow Oblast.

regions.label: The Upper Volga — Yaroslavl, Kostroma, Vladimir and Ivanovo
regions.sub: Yaroslavl, Kostroma, Vladimir, Ivanovo, Rybinsk, Uglich

eras.polity: Grand Principality of Moscow — the former Vladimir-Suzdal lands
eras.note: The Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal is dated 1157-1389. The area later formed Vladimirsky Uyezd of the Zamoskovny Krai.

eras.polity: Tsardom of Russia; Vladimir Province within Moscow Governorate from 1719
eras.note: Vladimir Province was formed in 1719 as part of Moscow Governorate.

eras.polity: Yaroslavl Viceroyalty (1777), Vladimir Viceroyalty (1778) and Kostroma Governorate (1796)
eras.note: Yaroslavl Governorate dates from 1777 and had ten uyezds; Vladimir became a governorate on 1 November 1796 with 13 uyezds from 1881 to 1917; Kostroma Governorate (1796 to 1929) had 12 uyezds, among them Galich, Kineshma, Makaryev, Soligalich and Vetluga.
Vladimir Governorate was abolished by a decree of 14 January 1929 effective 1 October 1929, and the Ivanovo Industrial Oblast was formed around Ivanovo.

eras.polity: Ivanovo Oblast and Yaroslavl Oblast (11 March 1936)
eras.note: On 11 March 1936 part of the Industrial Oblast became Ivanovo Oblast and the remainder was split off to create Yaroslavl Oblast.

regions.label: Smolensk and Bryansk
regions.sub: Smolensk, Vyazma, Bryansk, Roslavl, Gagarin, Klintsy

eras.note: Before registers. Bryansk came under Lithuania in 1356 and Moscow took it in 1503 after the Battle of Vedrosha; Smolensk was Lithuanian from 1404 until Vasily III took it in 1514.

eras.polity: Grand Principality of Moscow, from 1547 the Tsardom of Russia
eras.note: The fortress of Bryansk played a major role in the Time of Troubles (1598-1613).

Smolensk fell to the Commonwealth in 1611 after a siege of 1609-1611. The Truce of Deulino (dated 1618 or 1619 depending on the source) gave the southern and western parts of the present Bryansk Oblast to Poland, and Russia recaptured Smolensk in 1654.

eras.polity: Tsardom of Russia — Smolensk, and the Starodub regiment
eras.note: In 1654 Russia annexed the left bank of the Dnieper, including south-western Bryansk lands, organised in regiments of which Starodub was one of the largest. The Truce of Andrusovo in 1667 had the Commonwealth give up its claims to Smolensk.

eras.polity: Smolensk Governorate (1708); Kiev, Belgorod and Oryol governorates for Bryansk
eras.note: Smolensk became the seat of a governorate in 1708. The Bryansk, Karachev, Sevsk and Trubchevsk uyezds belonged to Kiev Governorate in 1709, Sevsk Province joined Belgorod Governorate in 1727, and Bryansk was moved to Oryol Governorate in 1779, so Bryansk-area families are filed under Oryol before 1920.

eras.polity: Bryansk Oblast (1920), Western Oblast (1929), Smolensk Oblast (1937)
eras.note: Bryansk Oblast was established on 1 April 1920 and absorbed into the Western Oblast on 1 October 1929. On 27 September 1937 the Western Krai was abolished and split into Smolensk and Oryol oblasts, with Bryansk's territory going to Oryol.

Smolensk was captured on 16 July 1941 and part of Smolensk Oblast was occupied until September 1943; the Bryansk region was occupied from August to October 1941 and liberated in August-September 1943.

eras.polity: Smolensk Oblast and Bryansk Oblast (re-established 5 July 1944)
eras.note: The modern Bryansk Oblast was re-established by decree on 5 July 1944.

regions.label: Kaluga, Tula and Oryol
regions.sub: Kaluga, Tula, Oryol, Yelets, Borovsk, Maloyaroslavets

eras.polity: Grand Principality of Moscow, from 1547 the Tsardom of Russia; from 1658 the Belgorod Razriad in the south
eras.note: The Belgorod Razriad, set up in 1658 with Belgorod and then Kursk as its centre, covered parts of the present Oryol, Kursk, Belgorod and Voronezh regions and was abolished on 18 December 1708.

eras.polity: Russian Empire — Kiev, then Belgorod Governorate (Oryol and Sevsk provinces)
eras.note: The Belgorod Razriad's towns went into Kiev Governorate in 1708. Belgorod Province was separated from it on 1 March 1727 and Oryol and Sevsk provinces were added to the Belgorod Governorate later that year; that governorate was abolished in 1779.

Oryol Governorate had uyezds including Yelets, Livny, Bryansk, Karachev, Sevsk and Trubchevsk and 2,033,798 inhabitants in 1897; Tula had 12 uyezds and Kaluga 11, among them Borovsk, Maloyaroslavets and Kozelsk. Tula Governorate ended in 1929 and Kaluga Governorate on 1 October 1929.

eras.polity: Central Black Earth Oblast (Oryol, 1928-1934), Moscow Oblast (Tula, Kaluga), then separate oblasts
eras.note: Oryol Governorate was merged into the Central Black Earth Oblast on 14 May 1928; Tula and Ryazan oblasts were separated from Moscow Oblast in September 1937, Oryol Oblast came out of the split of the Western Krai on 27 September 1937, and in 1944 districts went from Moscow Oblast to Kaluga Oblast.

regions.label: Ryazan and Tambov
regions.sub: Ryazan, Tambov, Lipetsk, Kasimov, Skopin, Spassk

eras.note: Before registers. The Principality of Ryazan is dated 1129-1521.

eras.polity: Grand Principality of Moscow, from 1547 the Tsardom of Russia
eras.note: Ryazan's principality ended in 1521. The central Muscovite records are in RGADA, Moscow.

eras.polity: Azov Governorate (1708), Voronezh Governorate (from 1725) — the Tambov and Shatsk provinces
eras.note: Azov Governorate was created on 29 December 1708 with its seat at Tambov until 1715, and in 1719 it was divided into five provinces including Tambov and Shatsk. It was renamed Voronezh Governorate in 1725 and abolished in 1779.

eras.polity: Tambov Viceroyalty (1779) and Tambov Governorate (1796); Ryazan Governorate (1796)
eras.note: Tambov Governorate had 12 uyezds and unchanged boundaries until 1926, when its northern half was split between Penza and Ryazan. Ryazan Governorate had 12 uyezds: Dankov, Yegoryevsk, Zaraysk, Kasimov, Mikhaylov, Pronsk, Ranenburg, Ryazhsk, Ryazan, Sapozhok, Skopin and Spassk.
