eras.polity: Central Black Earth Oblast (Tambov, 1928-1934); Central Industrial Oblast (Ryazan, 1929)
eras.note: A separatist 'Republic of Tambov' fought the Red Army from 1920 to 1922. Tambov Governorate was folded into the Central Black Earth Oblast in 1928 and Tambov Oblast formed in 1937; Ryazan Oblast was separated from Moscow Oblast in September 1937.

regions.label: The Black Earth south — Kursk, Belgorod and Voronezh
regions.sub: Kursk, Belgorod, Voronezh, Stary Oskol, Valuyki, Ostrogozhsk

eras.note: The Razriad had Belgorod and then Kursk as its centre and included Sloboda Cossack regiments; Cossacks settled under sloboda privileges and, from the early 1650s, Ukrainian border populations moved to free lands at the tsar's invitation.

eras.polity: Azov and Voronezh governorates (Voronezh); Kiev, then Belgorod Governorate (Belgorod, Kursk)
eras.note: Voronezh lay in the Azov Governorate of 1708, seated at Voronezh from 1715. Belgorod's towns went into Kiev Governorate in 1708, Belgorod Province became its own governorate on 1 March 1727, and that governorate was abolished in 1779.

eras.polity: Kursk Governorate (12 December 1796) and Voronezh Governorate (1796)
eras.note: Kursk Governorate had 15 uyezds in 1914, among them Belgorod, Staryi Oskol and Putivl (Putivl is now in Ukraine). Voronezh Governorate had nine uyezds in 1796 including Valuysky, gained Bogucharsky, Ostrogozhsky and Novokhopyorsky in 1802, and the transferred Starobelsky uyezd returned in 1824.

eras.polity: Central Black Earth Oblast (14 May 1928 to 13 June 1934), then Voronezh and Kursk oblasts
eras.note: The Central Black Earth Oblast, seated at Voronezh, was formed from the Voronezh, Kursk, Oryol and Tambov governorates and divided in 1934 between new Voronezh and Kursk oblasts.

regions.label: Nizhny Novgorod, Mordovia and Penza
regions.sub: Nizhny Novgorod, Arzamas, Lukoyanov, Penza, Saransk

eras.note: Before registers. Nizhny Novgorod was founded in 1221, passed into the Vladimir-Suzdal principality in 1264, and became the seat of the Suzdal principality in 1350.

eras.polity: Grand Principality of Moscow; part of the Mordvin lands under the Khanate of Kazan
eras.note: Moscow took Nizhny Novgorod in 1392. After the Golden Horde broke up, some Mordvins came under the Khanate of Kazan and others under Moscow.
The Mordvin lands came under the Russian crown with the annexation of the Khanate of Kazan in 1552.

eras.polity: Kazan Governorate, then Nizhny Novgorod Governorate and Penza Governorate
eras.note: Nizhny Novgorod was part of Kazan Governorate in 1708, became a governorate in 1714, merged back in 1717 and was re-created in 1719 (viceroyalty from 1779). Penza Governorate was established in 1780. Orthodox parish metrical books were made compulsory in 1722.

eras.polity: Nizhny Novgorod, Penza and Simbirsk governorates
eras.note: Mordovia was mainly administered from Penza Governorate, but Simbirsk and Nizhny Novgorod governorates each had an Ardatovsky uyezd, so the name alone does not say which governorate holds the record. The household returns of the 1897 census mostly did not survive.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Gorky Oblast and the Mordovian ASSR
eras.note: Penza Governorate was abolished in 1928 and Nizhny Novgorod Governorate in 1929. The Mordovian Okrug was founded in 1928, became an autonomous oblast in 1930 and an ASSR in 1934; Nizhny Novgorod was renamed Gorky in 1932 and regained its name in 1990.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Nizhny Novgorod and Penza oblasts, Republic of Mordovia
eras.note: The Mordovian ASSR was renamed the Republic of Mordovia in 1994.

regions.label: Kazan, Chuvashia and Mari El
regions.sub: Kazan, Chistopol, Sviyazhsk, Bolgary, Cheboksary, Yoshkar-Ola

eras.note: Before registers. The khanate's founding is dated 1437 or 1438 by some historians and 1445 by others; its peoples included Tatars, Chuvash, Mari and Udmurts.

eras.polity: Tsardom of Russia — Prikaz of the Kazan Palace
eras.note: Kazan was stormed on 2 October 1552 (Old Style). Part of the Mari population resisted until 1557, and Orthodox clergy baptised many Tatars by force.

Kazan Governorate was formed in 1708; Astrakhan (1717), Nizhny Novgorod (1719) and Orenburg (1744) were later taken out of it. Mosques in the area had been destroyed by 1593 and the ban on building them was lifted in the eighteenth century.

THE TRAP. Vyatka, Simbirsk and Ufa were separated from Kazan in 1781, so Menzelinsk (now in Tatarstan) belonged to Ufa Governorate and Bugulma to Samara Governorate. Muslim parishes answered to the Orenburg Muslim Spiritual Assembly in Ufa (founded 1788), and their metric books are in Old Tatar.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Tatar ASSR, Chuvash and Mari autonomies
eras.note: Kazan Governorate was abolished in 1920: its eastern part became the Tatar ASSR on 27 May 1920 and its western part was later divided between Chuvashia and Mari El.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Tatarstan, Chuvashia, Mari El
eras.note: Tatarstan declared sovereignty on 30 August 1990 and took the name Republic of Tatarstan in 1992.

regions.label: Vyatka, Udmurtia and the Perm Kama
regions.sub: Kirov (Vyatka), Izhevsk, Sarapul, Perm, Kudymkar

eras.note: Before registers. The founding of Khlynov, later Vyatka, is dated 1374, with earlier dates such as 1181 given in other sources.

eras.polity: Muscovy and the Tsardom of Russia — Kazan Governorate from 1708
eras.note: Moscow annexed the Vyatka land in 1489, and Udmurtia joined Russia without a war after Kazan fell in 1552. Perm began as the village of Yagoshikha, first mentioned in 1647, and a copper-smelting works there in 1723 is taken as the city's founding.

THE TRAP. Perm Governorate dates from 1781 and Vyatka Governorate from 1796, and Sarapul uyezd stayed in Vyatka Governorate until it was transferred to Perm Governorate on 4 November 1920. The Vyatka governorate covered roughly modern Kirov Oblast and Udmurtia.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Udmurt autonomy, Kirov and Perm (Molotov)
eras.note: The Votyak Autonomous Oblast was formed on 4 November 1920, renamed Udmurt in 1932 and made an ASSR in 1934. Vyatka became Kirov in 1934, and Perm was called Molotov from 1940 to 1957; Perm Governorate was abolished in 1923 into Ural Oblast.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Kirov Oblast, Udmurt Republic, Perm region
eras.note: The Udmurt ASSR was renamed the Udmurt Republic on 11 October 1991.

regions.label: Simbirsk and Samara — the Middle Volga
regions.sub: Ulyanovsk (Simbirsk), Syzran, Samara, Tolyatti, Sengiley

eras.note: Kazan fell in 1552, and the Kazan territory was run by the Prikaz of the Kazan Palace until the governorates of 1708.
Orenburg Governorate was created on 15 March 1744 from lands taken from the Siberian and Astrakhan governorates, and Simbirsk was separated from Kazan in 1781.
Simbirsk Governorate was established in 1796 with eight uyezds: Alatyr, Ardatov, Buinsk, Karsun, Kurmysh, Sengiley, Simbirsk and Syzran. Buinsk is now in Tatarstan and Alatyr in Chuvashia.

THE TRAP. Samara Governorate was established in 1850 (1851 on some sources) with seven uyezds: Bugulma, Buguruslan, Buzuluk, Nikolayevsk, Novouzensk, Samara and Stavropol, so Bugulma (now Tatarstan) and Buzuluk (now Orenburg Oblast) are filed under Samara, and Samara's Stavropol is Stavropol-on-Volga, not the Caucasus city. FamilySearch has a collection titled Russia, Samara, Church Books 1748-1934.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Middle Volga Oblast, Ulyanovsk and Kuybyshev regions
eras.note: Simbirsk was renamed Ulyanovsk in 1924. Samara Governorate was abolished on 14 May 1928, and Simbirsk Governorate's territory went to the Ulyanovsk, Mordovsk and Syzran okrugs of the Middle Volga Oblast.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Ulyanovsk and Samara oblasts

regions.label: Saratov and Volgograd — the Volga German colonies and Tsaritsyn
regions.sub: Saratov, Engels, Balashov, Kamyshin, Volgograd (Tsaritsyn)

eras.note: Tsaritsyn is documented as a fortress from 1589, though an earlier founding in 1555 is also given.

Astrakhan Governorate was cut from Kazan in 1717, and Saratov province was established within it in 1769. Catherine II's manifestos inviting European settlers date from 1762 and 1763, and the German colonies on the Volga were founded in 1764-1767.

THE TRAP. Tsaritsyn (Volgograd) lay in Tsaritsynsky uyezd of Saratov Governorate until 1919. A decree of 4 June 1871 repealed many privileges of the German colonists, and colonial self-government ended on 16 June 1871.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Volga German Labour Commune and ASSR; Tsaritsyn (Stalingrad)
eras.note: The Labour Commune of Volga Germans was set up in October 1918 and became an ASSR in 1924, with Engels (Pokrovsk before 1931) as capital. Tsaritsyn Governorate was split from Saratov in 1919, and the city was renamed Stalingrad in 1925.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Saratov and Stalingrad (Volgograd) oblasts
eras.note: The Volga German ASSR was abolished in September 1941 after the decree of 28 August, with transfers running from 3 to 20 September; its territory went to Saratov Oblast (15 cantons) and Stalingrad Oblast (7 cantons). Stalingrad was renamed Volgograd on 10 November 1961.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Saratov and Volgograd oblasts

regions.label: Astrakhan and the Kalmyk steppe
regions.sub: Astrakhan, Elista, Kharabali

eras.note: Before registers. The khanate is said to have been founded in 1466.
Russia occupied Astrakhan in 1556, and the city was moved about 12 km south to its present site in 1558.

eras.polity: Kalmyk Khanate on the lower Volga, beside Russian Astrakhan
eras.note: Oirats reached the lower Volga in 1630. In winter 1770-1771 Ubashi Khan led roughly 170,000 Kalmyks back toward Dzungaria, many on the right bank being left behind, and Catherine II abolished the khanate in October 1771.
Astrakhan Governorate was created on 3 December 1717 out of Kazan Governorate. Muslim parishes existed in the governorate in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.
Astrakhan Governorate was abolished on 21 May 1928 and absorbed into Lower Volga Oblast, later Lower Volga Krai.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Astrakhan Oblast and Kalmykia

regions.label: Bashkortostan and Orenburg
regions.sub: Ufa, Orenburg, Sterlitamak, Belebey, Orsk

eras.note: The Bashkirs joined Russia after the fall of Kazan in 1552; Bashkir councils sent delegations to the tsar in 1555-1557, and historians still debate whether this was voluntary. Bashkir rebellions followed in 1662-1664 and 1704-1711.

eras.polity: Orenburg Governorate (1744), Ufa Viceroyalty (1782), Orenburg Governorate (1796)
eras.note: Orenburg Governorate was created on 15 March 1744, became the Ufa Viceroyalty in 1782 and was renamed Orenburg Governorate in 1796, with Ufa the capital from 1802 to 1865. The Orenburg Cossack Host was formed in 1755, and the Orenburg Muslim Spiritual Assembly, which oversaw Muslim parishes, was founded in 1788.

THE TRAP. In 1865 Orenburg Governorate was split: Ufa Governorate took Belebey, Birsk, Zlatoust, Menzelinsk, Sterlitamak and Ufa uyezds, while Orenburg kept Orenburg, Orsk, Troitsk, Verkhneuralsk and Chelyabinsk. Zlatoust and Chelyabinsk are now in Chelyabinsk Oblast, Menzelinsk is in Tatarstan, and Buzuluk lay in Samara Governorate.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Bashkir ASSR and Orenburg
eras.note: Ufa Governorate was transformed into the Bashkir ASSR on 14 June 1922. Chelyabinsk Governorate was split from Orenburg in 1919, Orenburg Governorate was abolished on 14 May 1928, and the Orenburg Cossack Host ceased to exist in 1920.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Republic of Bashkortostan and Orenburg Oblast
eras.note: The Bashkir ASSR declared sovereignty on 11 October 1990 and was renamed the Republic of Bashkortostan on 25 February 1992.

regions.label: The Middle and South Urals — Yekaterinburg and Chelyabinsk
regions.sub: Yekaterinburg, Chelyabinsk, Nizhny Tagil, Zlatoust, Magnitogorsk

eras.polity: Russian Empire — the mining Urals and the Orenburg Expedition forts
eras.note: Yekaterinburg was founded on 18 November 1723, and the Demidov ironworks of Nevyansk and Tagil date to the 1700s-1720s. Forts of the Orenburg Expedition went up from 1734, and Chelyabinsk fortress became the centre of Iset Province in 1743.

eras.polity: Perm Governorate (Yekaterinburg, Shadrinsk) and Orenburg and Ufa governorates (Chelyabinsk, Troitsk, Zlatoust)
eras.note: THE TRAP. The Middle Urals had their own administration as Perm Governorate from 1781. Chelyabinsk uyezd was moved to the Ufa Viceroyalty in 1782 and stayed in Orenburg Governorate after 1865, while Zlatoust went to Ufa Governorate.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Yekaterinburg and Chelyabinsk governorates, then Ural Oblast
eras.note: Perm Governorate was split on 15 July 1919 and its eastern part became Yekaterinburg Governorate; Chelyabinsk Governorate was formed in 1919 from eastern Orenburg Governorate with Kurgan. Ural Oblast (1923-1934) merged the Perm, Yekaterinburg and Tyumen governorates.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Sverdlovsk and Chelyabinsk oblasts
eras.note: Sverdlovsk Oblast was established on 17 January 1934 and Chelyabinsk Oblast on the same date, with Chelyabinsk's present boundaries set in 1943 when Kurgan Oblast was detached. Yekaterinburg was renamed Sverdlovsk in 1924 and regained its name on 23 September 1991.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Sverdlovsk and Chelyabinsk oblasts

regions.label: The Don — Rostov and the Don Host
regions.sub: Rostov-on-Don, Taganrog, Novocherkassk, Azov, Shakhty

eras.note: Before registers. Cossack colonists came to the Don as the Golden Horde broke up; the sources cite the Battle of Shelon in 1471 and the fall of the Golden Horde in 1480.
Don and Zaporozhian Cossacks captured the Azov fortress in 1637, and its defence in 1641 is a key episode of Don Cossack history.
From 1786 the territory was officially called Don Host Land, and the Cossack capital moved to Novocherkassk in 1805.
The Don Host Oblast of 1870 lay across what is now Rostov Oblast and parts of Volgograd and Voronezh oblasts, so a Don Cossack family's papers may sit in more than one modern oblast.

eras.polity: Soviet Russia — Don region, North Caucasus and Azov-Black Sea krais
eras.note: Soviet decossackization began in 1919 and lasted into the following years.
Rostov Oblast was formed on 13 September 1937 from the Azov-Black Sea Krai.

regions.label: The Kuban — Krasnodar and Taman
regions.sub: Krasnodar, Temryuk, Novorossiysk, Sochi, Maykop

eras.note: Before registers. The Golden Horde ruled the area from 1243 to 1438.

eras.polity: Crimean Khanate, Circassia and the Ottoman Empire
eras.note: Parts of the Kuban were held by the Crimean Khanate, Circassia and the Ottoman Empire.

eras.polity: Russian Empire — Taman and the right bank of the Kuban
eras.note: In April 1783, after the Crimean Khanate was liquidated, a decree of Catherine II brought right-bank Kuban and the Taman Peninsula into the Russian Empire.

eras.polity: Black Sea Cossack Host and the Caucasus Line Host
eras.note: Former Zaporozhian Cossacks migrated to the Kuban in 1792-1793 as the Black Sea Cossack Host. The Caucasian Line Cossack Host was established on 25 October 1832, though Linear settlers had been on the Kuban since 1777.
The Kuban Cossack Host was formed by decree of 19 November 1860, merging the Caucasus Line and Black Sea hosts. During the Civil War the Kuban Cossacks proclaimed the Kuban People's Republic.

eras.polity: Soviet Russia — Kuban, North Caucasus and Azov-Black Sea krais
eras.note: Soviet decossackization fell on the Kuban Cossacks between 1919 and 1933.
Krasnodar Krai was formed on 13 September 1937 when the Azov-Black Sea Krai was divided between it and Rostov Oblast.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Krasnodar Krai and the Republic of Adygea
eras.note: Adygea is a republic entirely enclosed by the krai.

regions.label: Stavropol, Karachay-Cherkessia, Kabardino-Balkaria and North Ossetia
regions.sub: Stavropol, Pyatigorsk, Cherkessk, Nalchik, Vladikavkaz

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Russia — Azov-Mozdok fortress line, Caucasus Oblast (1822), Stavropol Governorate (1847)
eras.note: Stavropol was founded as a fortress on 22 October 1777 (Old Style) on the Azov-Mozdok line and became a district town in 1785. Ossetia was brought into the empire gradually between 1774 and 1806 and was fully controlled by 1830, while Kabarda was annexed in the Russo-Circassian War, dated 1769-1830 on one account.

The Caucasian War was declared over on 21 May (Old Style) 1864. The Terek Oblast, seated at Vladikavkaz, held districts including Nalchik, Nazran and Mozdok, and its creation is dated 1860 or 1873 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — North Caucasus Krai and autonomous oblasts
eras.note: North Ossetia became an autonomous oblast on 7 July 1924 and an ASSR on 5 December 1936. The North Caucasus Krai (17 October 1924) was renamed Ordzhonikidze Krai in March 1937 and Stavropol Krai on 12 January 1943.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Stavropol Krai and the autonomous republics
eras.note: The Karachays were deported in 1943 and the Balkars on 8 March 1944, to Central Asia.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Stavropol Krai, Karachay-Cherkessia, Kabardino-Balkaria, North Ossetia-Alania
eras.note: A brief Ossetian-Ingush conflict took place in the Prigorodny District in 1992.

regions.label: Chechnya, Ingushetia and Dagestan
regions.sub: Grozny, Nazran, Makhachkala, Derbent, Kizlyar

eras.note: Before registers. A 1724 treaty assigned Derbent to Russia but it returned to Persia in 1735; Russia took it again in 1796 and withdrew.

eras.polity: Russia — Treaty of Gulistan and the Caucasian War
eras.note: Persia ceded southern Dagestan, including Derbent, to Russia under the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813. Shamil led the Imamate of Dagestan from 1834 until his capture in 1859.

Dagestan Oblast was created in 1860 with its seat at Temir-Khan-Shura (now Buynaksk) and ended in 1920 or 1921 depending on the source. Grozny, Nazran and Kizlyar districts belonged to the Terek Oblast, not to Dagestan.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Dagestan ASSR and the Chechen-Ingush ASSR
eras.note: The Dagestan ASSR was proclaimed on 20 January 1921. Chechnya and Ingushetia were combined into the Chechen-Ingush ASSR.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Grozny Oblast; Chechens and Ingush deported
eras.note: Chechens and Ingush were deported from 23 February 1944, transports running to 13 March, mostly to Kazakhstan and Kirgizia. The Chechen-Ingush ASSR was dissolved into Grozny Oblast, and parts of its territory went to North Ossetia, Georgia and the Dagestan ASSR.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Chechen-Ingush ASSR restored; Dagestan ASSR
eras.note: The deportees were allowed to return from January 1957; the Chechen-Ingush ASSR was restored in its 1936 borders, in 1957 or 1958 depending on the source.
Ingushetia separated from the Chechen Republic after 1991.

regions.label: West Siberia — Tyumen, Tobolsk, Omsk, Khanty-Mansi
regions.sub: Tyumen, Tobolsk, Omsk, Kurgan, Khanty-Mansiysk, Surgut

eras.polity: Khanate of Sibir (successor to the Golden Horde)
eras.note: Before registers. The Khanate of Sibir fell to the Cossack expedition under Yermak, which set out in July 1581; the conquest is dated 1582.

eras.polity: Tsardom and Empire of Russia — Tyumen (1586) and Tobolsk (1587)
eras.note: Tyumen was founded in 1586 and Tobolsk in 1587. FamilySearch's Tobolsk church-books collection runs 1722-1930, so the collection reaches back to 1722.

eras.polity: Tobolsk Governorate — Tobolsk Viceroyalty, then the Siberian Governor-Generalship
eras.note: Tobolsk Governorate was formed in 1782 with Tobolsk and Tomsk oblasts and re-established in 1796. In 1804 part of its territory went to the new Tomsk Governorate.

Tobolsk Governorate was one of the governorates of the West Siberian Governor-Generalship from 1822 to 1882. In 1868 Omsk was transferred to Akmolinsk Oblast, so Omsk records after that date are filed under Akmolinsk, not Tobolsk.

eras.polity: Tobolsk Governorate — Tyumen and Tobolsk uyezds
eras.note: Trans-Siberian railway building and resettlement brought several million migrants east of the Urals between 1890 and 1914, so many families arrive in the registers late in this era. Metrical books were kept in two copies, one in the parish and one sent to the consistory.

eras.polity: Soviet Russia — Tobolsk Governorate, moved to Tyumen and renamed Tyumen Governorate in 1920
eras.note: The seat moved from Tobolsk to Tyumen in 1919-1920 and the governorate was renamed Tyumen Governorate in 1920. Civil registration (ZAGS) replaced church registration under the decree of 18 December 1917 (Old Style), and metric books are now kept in the State Archive.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Tyumen Oblast with the Khanty-Mansi and Yamalo-Nenets districts
eras.note: Tyumen Oblast was founded on 14 August 1944 and administers two autonomous okrugs, Khanty-Mansi and Yamalo-Nenets.

eras.polity: Russia — Tyumen, Omsk and Kurgan oblasts

regions.label: Tomsk, Novosibirsk and the Altai
regions.sub: Tomsk, Novosibirsk, Barnaul, Kemerovo, Biysk, Gorno-Altaysk

eras.polity: Mongol Empire and Golden Horde successors — Zunghar Khanate in the Altai
eras.note: Before registers. The Altai lands were held in turn by the Mongol Empire, the Golden Horde, Northern Yuan and the Zunghar Khanate. Russian Tomsk was founded in 1604.

eras.polity: Tsardom and Empire of Russia — Tomsk fort and its district
eras.note: Tomsk was founded in 1604. FamilySearch's Tomsk church-books collection, drawn from the State Archives of Tomsk Oblast, begins in 1752.

eras.polity: Tobolsk Governorate — Tomsk and Kolyvan oblasts
eras.note: Tomsk was an oblast of Tobolsk Governorate from 1782 and Kolyvan Oblast was added in 1796, so records of these years are in the Tobolsk series.

Tomsk Governorate covered most of today's Altai Krai, Altai Republic, Kemerovo, Novosibirsk and Tomsk oblasts and parts of Kazakhstan. About 2.8 million migrants moved east in 1908-1913 under the Stolypin reforms, and many settled this belt along the railway.

In 1917 the southern uyezds were cut off as Altai Governorate, and in 1921 the southwestern lands including Kainsk and Novonikolayevsk (later Novosibirsk) uyezds formed Novonikolayevsk Governorate. Tomsk Governorate was abolished on 25 May 1925.

eras.polity: Siberian Krai, then West Siberian Krai (from 30 July 1930), seat Novosibirsk
eras.note: West Siberian Krai had its seat at Novosibirsk and was disestablished on 28 September 1937. Its successors were Novosibirsk Oblast and Altai Krai.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Novosibirsk Oblast and Altai Krai
eras.note: Altai Krai was established on 28 September 1937. In 1942 families of men deported from Eastern Europe were sent to Altai Krai and some were held in Gulag labour camps.

eras.polity: Russia — Novosibirsk, Tomsk, Kemerovo and Altai Krai

regions.label: Yenisei Siberia — Krasnoyarsk, Khakassia and Tuva
regions.sub: Krasnoyarsk, Yeniseysk, Abakan, Minusinsk, Kyzyl, Kansk

eras.note: Before registers. Yeniseysk was founded in 1619 and Krasnoyarsk in 1628.

eras.polity: Tsardom and Empire of Russia — Krasnoyarsk and Yeniseysk forts, under Tomsk
eras.note: Yeniseysk Governorate was separated from Tomsk Governorate in 1822; before 1804 the Tomsk lands had been part of Tobolsk Governorate.

eras.polity: Yeniseysk Governorate (from 26 January/7 February 1822), seat Krasnoyarsk
eras.note: The governorate was set up in 1822 with five okrugs: Krasnoyarsk, Yeniseysk (with the Turukhansk territory), Achinsk, Minusinsk and Kansk, and placed in the East Siberian Governor-Generalship. Uryankhay Krai (roughly modern Tuva) became a Russian protectorate on 17 April 1914 and joined the governorate.

eras.polity: Yeniseysk Governorate under Soviet power; Tannu Tuva independent from 1921
eras.note: The Tannu Tuvan People's Republic was proclaimed on 14 August 1921, ending the governorate's claim on Tuva. Khakassky Uyezd was created on 14 November 1923, and the governorate was dissolved on 25 May 1925 into Siberian Krai.

eras.polity: Siberian Krai, East Siberian Krai (1930), Krasnoyarsk Krai (7 December 1934)
eras.note: Krasnoyarsk Okrug was moved to East Siberian Krai on 11 August 1930, and Krasnoyarsk Krai was created on 7 December 1934 by splitting the West and East Siberian krais. Tuva stayed a separate state, renamed the Tuvan People's Republic in 1926, until it joined the USSR on 1 November 1944.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Krasnoyarsk Krai and the Tuvan Autonomous Oblast
eras.note: Tuva was a Tuvan Autonomous Oblast of the Russian SFSR from 1944 and became the Tuvan ASSR on 10 October 1961. The region was used for exile under both tsarist and Soviet rule.

eras.polity: Russia — Krasnoyarsk Krai, Khakassia and Tuva
eras.note: Khakassia separated from Krasnoyarsk Krai in 1991 and became a republic. The Evenk and Taymyr okrugs were merged into the krai on 1 January 2007.

regions.label: Irkutsk, the Angara and Lake Baikal
regions.sub: Irkutsk, Angarsk, Bratsk, Ust-Kut, Slyudyanka, Bodaibo

eras.note: Before registers. Russian expansion east followed the conquest of the Khanate of Sibir in 1582, and Irkutsk was founded in 1661.

eras.polity: Tsardom and Empire of Russia — Irkutsk fort and its district

eras.note: Yakutsk was a region of Irkutsk Governorate from 1784 to 1805, Kamchatka was part of it from 1803, and Transbaikal stayed in it until 1851. Irkutsk became the seat of the Siberian Governor-Generalship in 1803.

Decembrists were exiled to settlements and colonies in this region from the 1830s, and the Trans-Siberian railway reached the oblast in 1898. Irkutsk synagogue metrical books for 1878-1920 are reported in the State Archive of Irkutsk Oblast.

eras.polity: Soviet Russia — Irkutsk Governorate (to 1926), then the East Siberian region
eras.note: Irkutsk Governorate lasted until 1926. East Siberian Krai had its seat at Irkutsk from 1930, and on 26 September 1937 its region was split into Irkutsk and Chita oblasts.
The Ust-Orda Buryat Okrug lay inside the oblast.

regions.label: Transbaikal — Buryatia and Zabaykalsky
regions.sub: Ulan-Ude, Chita, Nerchinsk, Kyakhta, Petrovsk-Zabaykalsky

eras.polity: Before registers — Buryat and Evenk lands
eras.note: Before registers. Cossacks and tsarist officials began moving into western Buryat lands in 1625, and the fort of Udinskoye, later Verkhneudinsk and now Ulan-Ude, was founded in 1666.

eras.polity: Russian Empire — Transbaikal in Irkutsk Governorate
eras.note: Kyakhta became the border crossing for Russia-China trade in 1727, Buddhism was recognised as an official religion of the empire in 1741, and the first Pandito Khambo Lama was elected in 1764. The Orthodox metrical books predominantly cover the Orthodox community, so Buddhist families may not appear in them.

Transbaikal Oblast was split from Irkutsk Governorate in 1851 with the Verkhneudinsk and Nerchinsk districts, so earlier records are in Irkutsk. It passed to the Amur Governor-Generalship in 1884 and to the Irkutsk Governor-Generalship in 1906; the 1897 census counted about 672,000 people, with large Buddhist and Old Believer communities.

eras.polity: Revolution and civil war — the oblast abolished in 1917
eras.note: Transbaikal Oblast was abolished during the 1917 revolution and re-established in 1920.

The Far Eastern Republic was proclaimed at Verkhneudinsk, which was its capital until October 1920, and then Chita. It joined the RSFSR on 15 November 1922, and Transbaikal Oblast, restored in 1920, was succeeded by Transbaikal Governorate.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Buryat ASSR and Chita Oblast
eras.note: The Buryat Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was created in 1923, Verkhneudinsk was renamed Ulan-Ude in 1934, and Chita Oblast was created on 26 September 1937 from the East Siberian region. Aga Buryatia and Ust-Orda Buryatia were detached from the Buryat-Mongolian ASSR in 1937.

eras.polity: Russia — Republic of Buryatia and Chita territory
eras.note: Buryatia declared sovereignty in 1990 and took the name Republic of Buryatia in 1992.

regions.label: Yakutia (Sakha) and the Lena
regions.sub: Yakutsk, Mirny, Lensk, Olekminsk, Verkhoyansk, Tiksi

eras.polity: Before registers — Yakut, Evenk, Even and Yukaghir lands
eras.note: Before registers. Yakutsk was founded in 1632.

eras.polity: Tsardom and Empire of Russia — Yakutsk uyezd (1638)
eras.note: The Yakutsk uyezd was formed in 1638 and became Yakutsk Province in 1775.

eras.polity: Yakutsk Province, then a region of Irkutsk Governorate (1784)
eras.note: From 1784 to 1805 Yakutsk was a region of Irkutsk Governorate, so records of these years are in the Irkutsk series.

The oblast was separated from Irkutsk Governorate in 1805 and divided into five uyezds in 1822. The Uda District was transferred to Primorskaya Oblast in 1857. Exile placement here ended in 1900, except for those convicted of crimes against religion or the state.
In April 1920 the oblast was annexed to Irkutsk Governorate as a special region, and in August 1920 its administrative independence was restored. The Yakut ASSR was formed on 27 April 1922.
Dalstroy, the forced-labour construction agency, ran from 13 November 1931 to 29 May 1957 and covered parts of Yakutia as well as the Magadan region and Chukotka.
Most of the former Yakutsk Oblast makes up the Sakha Republic.

regions.label: The Amur and Primorye — Blagoveshchensk, Khabarovsk, Vladivostok
regions.sub: Blagoveshchensk, Khabarovsk, Vladivostok, Nikolayevsk-on-Amur, Birobidzhan, Ussuriysk

eras.polity: Before registers — Daur, Ducher and Evenk lands
eras.note: Before registers. The Manchus conquered the area in 1639-1640.

eras.polity: Qing China, with Russian settlement from the mid-17th century
eras.note: The Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689) returned the Amur area to Qing control. Primorskaya Oblast was nonetheless created by the Russian Senate on 31 October 1856, and Blagoveshchensk was founded in 1856.

eras.polity: Amur Oblast (1858, seat Blagoveshchensk) and Primorskaya Oblast
eras.note: The Treaty of Aigun (28 May 1858) ceded the left bank of the Amur to Russia, and the Peking Convention of 1860 gave Russia the Ussuri region and Primorye. Primorskaya Oblast's capital was Nikolayevsk-on-Amur until 1880, then Khabarovka (now Khabarovsk).

eras.polity: Amur Governor-Generalship; Primorskaya capital Vladivostok from 1888
eras.note: Sakhalin became a separate administrative territory in 1884 and Transbaikal passed to the Amur Governor-Generalship the same year. Primorskaya Oblast was governed from Vladivostok from 1888 to 1922.

The Far Eastern Republic included the Transbaikal, Amur and Maritime provinces and the northern half of Sakhalin. Japan backed a White coup in Vladivostok in May 1921, the Red Army retook Vladivostok on 25 October 1922 and the republic merged into the RSFSR on 15 November 1922.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Primorskaya Governorate, Far Eastern Krai, Khabarovsk Krai
eras.note: The Amur territory was split in January 1926 between East Siberian and Far Eastern krais, Amur Oblast was established on 20 October 1932, and in 1938 its Far Eastern part passed to Khabarovsk Krai. Amur Oblast became independent within the RSFSR in 1948.

eras.polity: Russia — Amur Oblast, Khabarovsk and Primorsky krais

regions.label: Sakhalin — Russian and Japanese Karafuto
regions.sub: Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk (Toyohara), Aleksandrovsk-Sakhalinsky, Okha, Korsakov, Nogliki

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Joint Russian and Japanese residence under the Treaty of Shimoda
eras.note: The Treaty of Shimoda (1855) allowed Russian and Japanese nationals to live on the island without a boundary. Russia set up a penal colony (katorga) in 1857.

eras.polity: Russia — the Treaty of Saint Petersburg gave Russia the whole island
eras.note: By the Treaty of Saint Petersburg (1875) Japan gave up its Sakhalin claims in exchange for the Kuril Islands. Sakhalin became a separate administrative territory in 1884, and the katorga settlements were visited by Anton Chekhov in 1891.

eras.polity: Japan — Karafuto south of 50 degrees N; the north stayed Russian then Soviet
eras.note: THE TRAP. The Treaty of Portsmouth (1905) gave the southern half to Japan as Karafuto: civil administration from 28 August 1905, prefecture from 1 April 1907, capital Toyohara from 1908. The northern half stayed Russian; it was counted in the Far Eastern Republic in 1920, and Japan occupied it until 1925.

The Soviet invasion of southern Sakhalin began on 11 August 1945 and Toyohara was occupied on 25 August. Japanese residents were repatriated from December 1946 to July 1949 (279,356 people), Japan abolished the Karafuto prefecture on 1 June 1949, and Koreans who stayed formed the later Korean community.

regions.label: Kamchatka, Kolyma and Chukotka
regions.sub: Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Magadan, Anadyr, Okhotsk, Bolsheretsk

eras.polity: Before registers — Itelmen, Koryak, Even and Chukchi lands
eras.note: Before registers. Ivan Moskvitin reached the Sea of Okhotsk in 1639 and Okhotsk was founded in 1647.

eras.polity: Tsardom and Empire of Russia — Okhotsk, Anadyr and Kamchatka outposts
eras.note: Vladimir Atlasov explored Kamchatka in 1697-1699, Bolsheretsk was founded in 1703 and Petropavlovsk in 1740. A smallpox epidemic in 1768-1769 sharply reduced the Itelmen population.

eras.polity: Kamchatka Oblast within Irkutsk Governorate (1803), abolished 1822, re-established 1849
eras.note: Kamchatka Oblast was created in 1803 as part of Irkutsk Governorate with Petropavlovsk as capital from 1812. It was replaced in 1822 by the Kamchatka Maritime Administration, re-established in 1849 and absorbed into Primorskaya Oblast in 1856.
The administrative region of Anadyr was created in 1888.
Kamchatka Oblast was separated from Primorskaya Oblast on 30 June 1909 with Petropavlovsk, Okhotsk, Gizhiginsky and Anadyr uyezds and the Commander Islands. A Chukotka Uyezd was formed in 1909.

eras.polity: Soviet Russia — Kamchatka Governorate (1922), Chukotka National Okrug (1930), Dalstroy
eras.note: Dalstroy, a forced-labour agency, was established on 13 November 1931 and used Magadan as its base. Its prisoner numbers at the start of the year rose from 11,100 in 1932 to a peak of 199,726 in 1952.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Magadan Oblast and Kamchatka
eras.note: Magadan Oblast was established on 3 December 1953 and Dalstroy was dissolved on 29 May 1957. Kamchatka was declared a military zone after 1945 and stayed closed to unauthorised Soviet citizens until 1989 and to foreigners until 1990.

eras.polity: Russia — Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka Krai, Chukotka Autonomous Okrug
eras.note: Chukotka separated from Magadan Oblast in 1991 or 1992, depending on the source.

regions.label: Volhynia
regions.sub: Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Volodymyr, Kovel

eras.polity: Poland in the west, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the east
eras.note: Before registers. After Galicia-Volhynia broke up, Poland took western Volhynia and Lithuania the east; sources date the division between 1352 and 1366.

The voivodeship was ceded to the Polish Crown in 1569, but it did not cover all historic Volhynia: Zhytomyr and Ovruch belonged to the Kiev Voivodeship. A small south-western part (including Belz) went to Austria in 1772.

Eastern and central Volhynia became the governorate in 1795 (one source gives no separate creation date); the western part went to Austria's West Galicia. After annexation Greek Catholic church buildings were handed to the Russian Orthodox Church. Zhytomyr metrical books for 1795-1916 are in a FamilySearch collection, and Mennonite colony records begin in 1783.

eras.polity: Ukrainian People's Republic, then Polish and Soviet fronts
eras.note: A front line ran just west of Lutsk in 1917-18. In 1919 Poland held the area as the Volhynian District, and the Treaty of Riga in 1921 divided it.

eras.polity: Poland - Volhynian Voivodeship (Lutsk); Soviet Ukraine in the east
eras.note: Poland received the larger western part, organised as the Volhynian Voivodeship (1921-1939), with Lutsk as capital and Rivne its largest city. The rest, including Zhytomyr, stayed in the Ukrainian SSR, so one family's records can sit on both sides of the 1921 line.

eras.polity: Soviet annexation of the Polish part
eras.note: The Soviet Union invaded Poland on 17 September 1939 and occupied the Polish part of Volhynia.

eras.polity: German occupation - Reichskommissariat Ukraine (Wolhynien und Podolien)
eras.note: The Reichskommissariat was set up on 20 August 1941 with Rivne (Rovno) as its de facto capital. The 1943 massacres of Poles by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army in Volhynia fall in this period.
Soviet civil registration offices (ZAGS) date from 1918-19 depending on the source; Soviet-era civil registers are held by registry offices and the oblast state archives, not the church archives.

regions.label: Podolia
regions.sub: Kamianets-Podilskyi, Vinnytsia, Khmelnytskyi, Bar, Haisyn

eras.polity: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth - Podolian and Bracław Voivodeships
eras.note: After Vytautas died in 1430 Podolia was joined to the Podolian Voivodeship; the east (Bracław) stayed with Lithuania until the Union of Lublin in 1569 moved it to Poland.
The eyalet had its centre at Kamaniçe (Kamianets-Podilskyi) and sanjaks at Bar, Mejibuji and Yazlovets; it returned to Poland in 1699 (dated to the Treaty of Karlowitz).
The Poles abolished the Cossack regimental system on the right bank in 1699. Austria took the western part of Podolia in 1772, so a Podolian ancestor may have been Austrian from then.
Created in 1793 from the eastern parts annexed in the second partition. Its 1906 population was estimated at 3,543,700, with a significant Jewish minority.

eras.polity: Ukrainian People's Republic and West Ukrainian People's Republic; Polish and Soviet armies
eras.note: Western Podolia joined the West Ukrainian People's Republic after November 1918; Poland took control in 1919 and the Soviets held Podolia briefly in 1920. The Peace of Riga left western Podolia under Poland and eastern Podolia under the USSR.

eras.polity: Ukrainian SSR (and Moldavian ASSR, 1922-1940); Polish Tarnopol Voivodeship in the west
eras.note: The Moldavian ASSR existed in the south-west of Podolia from 1922 to 1940. The Holodomor of 1932-33 fell hardest on Vinnytsia, among other oblasts. The Polish western part joined Soviet Ukraine after the invasion of 17 September 1939.

eras.polity: German Reichskommissariat Ukraine; Romanian-held Transnistria in the south
eras.note: Romania held the area between the Southern Bug below Vinnytsia and the Dniester as Transnistria. From July 1941 Einsatzgruppen shot Podolia's Jewish population in mass killings.

eras.polity: Soviet Union - Ukrainian and Moldavian SSRs
Ukraine (north-eastern Moldova holds the Dniester left bank)
eras.note: Podolia lies in Ukraine and in north-eastern Moldova (northern Transnistria).

regions.label: Kyiv and the middle Dnieper
regions.sub: Kyiv, Cherkasy, Uman, Berdychiv, Brovary, Pereiaslav

eras.note: The Khmelnytsky uprising began in 1648 and the Hetmanate placed itself under the tsar at Pereiaslav in 1654.

eras.polity: Left bank: Cossack Hetmanate under Moscow; right bank: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
eras.note: THE TRAP. The Treaty of Andrusovo (1667) split the Hetmanate along the Dnieper, and the right bank was occupied by the Ottomans from 1672 to 1699. Which bank your village stood on decides which state, and which archive, made the record. A Kyiv Governorate existed 1708-1764.

eras.polity: Russia (left bank: Little Russia Governorate); Commonwealth (right bank)
eras.note: The hetmanship was abolished in 1764 and the left bank became the Little Russia Governorate, whose last Cossack administrative remnants ended in 1781. The right bank passed to Russia in the partitions of the 1790s.

The governorate was created by edict of 30 November 1796 (in effect 29 August 1797) and covered the right bank, with twelve uyezds including Uman, Cherkasy, Berdychiv and Skvyra. Parts of today's Kyiv oblast on the left bank lay in Chernigov Governorate instead. Kyiv consistory duplicates of the metrical books are at the Central State Historical Archives of Ukraine in Kyiv.

eras.polity: Ukrainian People's Republic, Ukrainian State, Soviet Ukraine
eras.note: The Ukrainian State and the Ukrainian Soviet Republic were both proclaimed in 1918, and Ukraine became part of the USSR in 1922.

eras.polity: Ukrainian SSR - Kiev Governorate abolished 1925, Kyiv Oblast 1932
eras.note: The governorate was abolished on 6 June 1925 and the Kyiv okruha became an oblast in 1932. Kyiv, Kharkiv, Vinnytsia and others took the largest losses in the Holodomor of 1932-33.

eras.polity: German occupation - Reichskommissariat Ukraine (General District Kiew)
eras.note: The Reichskommissariat was established on 20 August 1941 with civil administration from 1 September 1941; Kyiv was its de jure capital and Rivne the de facto one.

regions.label: Chernihiv and Poltava (the Left Bank)
regions.sub: Chernihiv, Poltava, Nizhyn, Hlukhiv, Konotop, Pereiaslav

eras.note: Founded in 1648; Baturyn and Chyhyryn were its early capitals.

The Left Bank kept autonomy under Moscow after 1667. Mazepa was hetman from 1687 to 1708, the Battle of Poltava was fought on 8 July 1709, and Hlukhiv was the capital from 1708 to 1764; Peter I created the Collegium of Little Russia in 1722.

The hetman post was abolished in 1764 and the territory became the Little Russia Governorate, which ran to 1781. In 1796 the Kiev Viceroyalty was split into the Kiev and Little Russia Governorates, and Little Russia was disbanded in 1802.

eras.polity: Russian Empire - Chernigov and Poltava Governorates
eras.note: Chernigov Governorate was created in 1802 from the disbanded Little Russia Governorate. It took in a large part of today's Sumy oblast and a large part of today's Bryansk oblast in Russia, so some Chernigov records now sit across the border. Originals or copies of Chernihiv records are at the State Archives of the Chernihiv region.
Called Chernihiv Governorate within the Ukrainian successor states from 1918 to 1925. In 1919 four northern counties (Mhlyn, Novozybkiv, Starodub and Surazh) were moved to Gomel Governorate.
The governorate was abolished in 1925 and divided among the Hlukhiv, Konotop, Nizhyn and Chernihiv okruhas. Chernihiv was among the oblasts with the largest losses in the Holodomor of 1932-33.
The Red Army liberated most of the occupied territory in 1943-1944.

regions.label: Sloboda Ukraine (Kharkiv region)
regions.sub: Kharkiv, Sumy, Izium, Kupiansk, Okhtyrka, Starobilsk

eras.note: Five regimental districts were named for their main towns: Ostrogozhsk, Kharkiv, Okhtyrka, Sumy and Izyum. Sumy was the capital until 1743, administration passed to a Russian prikaz in 1688, and Slavo-Serbia existed to the south from 1753 to 1764.
The regiments were disbanded and Cossack privileges abolished by the decree of 28 July 1765.

eras.polity: Kharkov Viceroyalty, then Sloboda Ukrainian Governorate
eras.note: The governorate became the Kharkov Viceroyalty in 1780 and was renamed the Sloboda Ukrainian Governorate in 1796.

When the province was abolished in 1835 most of its territory went to the new Kharkov Governorate and parts went to Voronezh and Kursk. Old Sloboda lands such as Valuyki, Ostrogozhsk, Sudzha and Shebekino are now in Russia.

eras.polity: Ukrainian People's Republic, Ukrainian State and civil war
eras.note: The Ukrainian State and the Ukrainian Soviet Republic were both proclaimed in 1918; the Provisional Workers' and Peasants' Government of Ukraine sat at Sudzha in November-December 1918.

eras.polity: Ukrainian SSR (Kharkiv its capital 1919-1934) and RSFSR
eras.note: Kharkiv was the capital of Soviet Ukraine from 1919 to 1934. The old Sloboda lands were split between the Ukrainian SSR and the RSFSR, and Kharkiv was among the oblasts with the largest losses in the Holodomor of 1932-33.
Germany occupied the region from 1941-42 until 1943.

regions.label: Novorossiya and the Donbas
regions.sub: Odesa, Mykolaiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk, Kherson

eras.polity: Crimean Khanate (Ottoman vassal), Nogai Horde, Zaporozhian Sich; Moldavia in the west
eras.note: Before registers. The Crimean Khanate controlled the northern Black Sea shore, the Nogai Horde settled the steppe in the sixteenth century, and Moldavia and Lithuania held the western areas.
Founded in 1764 with its centre at the Fortress of St Elizabeth, moved to Kremenchuk in 1765. Ottoman territories were annexed to it in 1774, and the Zaporozhian Sich was liquidated in 1775.

The governorate was dissolved in 1783. In 1792 a Russian-ruled 'New Moldavia' was declared between the Dniester and the Bug, Odesa was founded in 1794, and Novorossiya was re-established in 1796 with Ekaterinoslav as capital.

eras.polity: Russian Empire - Yekaterinoslav, Kherson and Taurida Governorates
eras.note: Novorossiya was split into the Yekaterinoslav, Kherson and Taurida governorates in 1802; a Novorossiysk-Bessarabia General Government sat at Odesa from 1822 to 1873. The mainland part of Taurida (Berdyansk, Dnieper and Melitopol uyezds) belongs here, not with Crimea. Catherine invited Romanians, Bulgarians, Serbs, Greeks, Albanians, Germans, Poles and others as colonists. Odesa church books for 1780-1898 are in a FamilySearch collection.

eras.polity: Ukrainian State, White governments, Ukrainian SSR
eras.note: The area was in the Ukrainian State and the Ukrainian Soviet Republic in 1918; White governments held parts in 1918-1920, and Soviet control followed. It became part of the Ukrainian SSR in 1922.
The Holodomor of 1932-33 took its largest losses in oblasts that include Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa and Stalino (now Donetsk).
General Districts Nikolajew and Dnjepropetrowsk lay in the Reichskommissariat Ukraine. Romania held the area between the Southern Bug and the Dniester as Transnistria.

Parts of Donetsk and Luhansk have been outside Ukrainian government control since 2014, and Russia annexed Kherson and Zaporizhzhia after 2022, though they remain internationally recognised as Ukrainian. Check archive access before planning a visit.

regions.label: Crimea
regions.sub: Simferopol, Sevastopol, Kerch, Yalta, Feodosia

eras.note: Before registers. The Crimean Khanate, a vassal of the Ottomans, controlled the northern Black Sea shore.
Russia annexed the Khanate in 1783 and established the Taurida Oblast soon after; it was abolished in 1796 and re-established as a governorate in 1802.

The governorate included mainland districts (Berdyansk, Dnieper, Melitopol) as well as the peninsula, so a 'Taurida' record may belong to either. Sevastopol and Kerch were city authorities and Yalta became a gradonachalstvo in 1914.

eras.polity: Crimean People's Republic (13 December 1917), then Soviet rule - Crimean ASSR from 1921
eras.note: The Bolsheviks overran Crimea in winter 1917-18, and a Crimean Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic is listed for 1921-1945.
The mainland section (Taurien) passed to civil administration in September 1942.

eras.polity: RSFSR - Crimean ASSR, then Crimean Oblast
eras.note: The Crimean Tatars were deported on 18-20 May 1944, and Armenians, Bulgarians and Greeks were also removed from Crimea. The Crimean ASSR was abolished on 30 June 1945.
Crimea was transferred from the RSFSR to the Ukrainian SSR in 1954. The ban on the Crimean Tatars' return was declared void on 14 November 1989.

eras.polity: Republic of Crimea under Russian administration
eras.note: Crimea has been administered by Russia since 2014.

regions.label: Bessarabia and the Dniester
regions.sub: Chisinau, Balti, Cahul, Soroca, Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, Izmail

eras.note: Before registers. The Ottomans ruled Khotyn directly.

The Treaty of Bucharest, signed 28 May 1812, ceded the land between the Prut and the Dniester to Russia. Bessarabia became an oblast in 1818, and the Novorossiysk-Bessarabia General Government sat at Odesa from 1822 to 1873.

eras.polity: Russia, with southern Bessarabia returned to Moldavia
eras.note: THE TRAP. The Treaty of Paris (1856) returned southern Bessarabia to Moldavia after the Crimean War, so for these years Cahul and Izmail records are Moldavian, not Russian. Russian rule was restored over the whole region in 1878.
Bessarabia became a governorate (guberniya) in 1873.

Sfatul Tarii declared independence on 6 February 1918 (24 January old style) and voted for union with Romania on 9 April 1918 (27 March old style). The Moldavian ASSR lay across the Dniester within Soviet Ukraine from 1922 to 1940.

Romania withdrew under Soviet pressure in 1940. The core joined parts of the Moldavian ASSR to form the Moldavian SSR, while northern and southern districts (including the Khotyn and Budjak areas) went to the Ukrainian SSR.

eras.polity: Romania - reconquered 1941, with Transnistria across the Dniester
eras.note: Romania recaptured the region in 1941 and lost it in 1944. A Transnistria Governorate lay across the Dniester.

eras.polity: Soviet Union - Moldavian SSR, and Ukrainian SSR (north and south)
Moldova; Ukraine (Khotyn and Budjak); Transnistria unrecognised
eras.note: The Moldavian and Ukrainian SSRs proclaimed independence in 1991. A Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic was proclaimed in Transnistria after a short war in the early 1990s, so records from the left bank may sit outside the national archive.

regions.label: Grodno, Brest and Navahrudak
regions.sub: Hrodna, Brest, Pinsk, Navahrudak, Slonim

eras.polity: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth - Grand Duchy of Lithuania
eras.note: Parish record-keeping here dates from the sixteenth century and is tied to the 1596 Union of Brest and the Uniate Church; registers were kept separately for each confession.

Minsk Governorate was created on 23 March 1793 and included Navahrudak and Pinsk uyezds; Grodno went to Russia in 1795 and Brest-Litovsk is dated to 1793 or 1795 depending on the source. The National Historical Archives of Belarus hold the metrical books in Minsk and its Grodno branch, not the regional archives; revision lists from the 5th (1795) to the 10th (1858) are in Minsk.

The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk was signed on 3 March 1918 and the Belarusian People's Republic proclaimed three weeks later. In 1920 Poland controlled the Novogrudok, Pinsk, Baranovichi and Nesvizh uyezds.

eras.polity: Poland - Polesie, Nowogrodek and Bialystok Voivodeships
eras.note: The Peace of Riga (1921) gave Poland Western Belorussia. Pinsk lay in Polesie Voivodeship and Navahrudak in Nowogrodek Voivodeship.
The USSR invaded on 17 September 1939; a People's Assembly voted on 30 October 1939 to join the BSSR, accepted on 2 and 12 November. Arrests and deportations followed in 1939-41.
The German army entered on 22 June 1941, and most of the region became part of Reichskommissariat Ostland.

The Bialystok region went to Poland in 1945 and the rest of Western Belorussia was kept in the BSSR. Civil registration offices (ZAGS) were established in 1918, a name still used in Russia and Belarus; many church records were confiscated and later moved to state archives.
Reading-room visits to the National Historical Archives of Belarus need an appointment, and a certificate confirming holdings is free.

regions.label: Minsk, Vitebsk, Mogilev and Gomel
regions.sub: Minsk, Vitebsk, Mogilev, Gomel, Mozyr, Bobruisk

eras.polity: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth - Grand Duchy of Lithuania
eras.note: Registers were kept separately by confession; their start here is tied to the 1596 Union of Brest and the Uniate Church.

eras.polity: Russian Empire - Vitebsk, Mogilev and Minsk governorates
eras.note: The first partition (1772) gave Russia the east, including Vitebsk and Mogilev; the Minsk Governorate came from the second partition and was created on 23 March 1793. In 1843 Vileysky and Disnensky uyezds passed from Minsk to Vilna Governorate. The National Historical Archives of Belarus in Minsk hold the Minsk and Mogilev consistory funds and the revision lists of 1795-1858.

eras.polity: Belarusian People's Republic (1918), then Soviet rule
eras.note: The Belarusian People's Republic was proclaimed three weeks after the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (3 March 1918); Minsk Governorate was abolished in 1921.
A WWII bomb destroyed metric books held at the Minsk Civil Registry Office.

regions.label: Armenia (Erivan)
regions.sub: Yerevan, Gyumri (Alexandropol), Vagharshapat (Echmiadzin), Gavar, Vardenis

eras.note: Before registers. The Khanates of Erivan and Nakhichevan were held by Persia until 1828.

The Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828) ceded the Erivan and Nakhichevan khanates. The Armenian Oblast was a separate unit from 1828 to 1840, then merged into other Transcaucasian provinces. A FamilySearch collection of Armenian church books from the Armenian Central Historical Archive runs 1838-1929.

The governorate was created in 1849 and also took in Nakhchivan and what is now Turkey's Igdir, so some records are in Azerbaijan or Turkey. Kars and Ardahan were kept by Russia after 1878. About 250,000 Armenians from Van and Alashkert retreated to the Russian frontier in June 1915.
Declared on 28 May 1918 after the Transcaucasian federation voted for independence on 22 April 1918. Soviet forces took over in December 1920.
The Transcaucasian federation was formed on 12 March 1922, renamed on 13 December 1922, admitted to the USSR on 30 December 1922 and dissolved on 5 December 1936.

regions.label: Georgia (Tiflis and Kutaisi)
regions.sub: Tbilisi (Tiflis), Kutaisi, Batumi, Telavi, Poti

eras.note: Kartli and Kakheti were united under Heraclius II in 1762. The Treaty of Georgievsk of 24 July 1783 made it a Russian protectorate, Tbilisi was sacked by Qajar Iran in 1795, and annexation is dated to Paul I's decree of 18 December 1800 or Alexander I's confirmation of 12 September 1801. West Georgia is filed under the later Kutaisi Governorate.

eras.polity: Russian Empire - Tiflis and Kutaisi Governorates
eras.note: Kutaisi Governorate was formed in 1846 from the Georgia-Imeretia Governorate, and Akhaltsikhe uyezd was ceded to Tiflis in 1867. Lands around Batum were added from 1878, and two Batum districts became Batum Oblast in 1903. Parish registers of the early nineteenth century to 1921 are in the Georgian State Historical Archive, and FamilySearch lists Tiflis Jewish community registers for 1886-1920.
Georgia declared independence on 26 May 1918. The Red Army invasion began on 12 February 1921 (one source gives 11 February) and Tbilisi fell on 25 February.
The Transcaucasian federation was formed on 12 March 1922 and dissolved on 5 December 1936.
Civil registration (ZAGS) from the 1920s onward is the most complete source for the Soviet period; access to recent records may be restricted.

regions.label: Newfoundland (the island)
regions.sub: St. John's, Harbour Grace, Placentia, Bonavista, Burin, Fogo

eras.note: John Cabot landed on the northeast coast in 1497 (the site is not known) and Humphrey Gilbert took possession at St John's for England in August 1583; Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows dates to about 1000. Settlement under a company began in 1610.

The London and Bristol Company settled Cuper's Cove in 1610, Avalon became a province in 1623, and Sir David Kirke became the first governor over all Newfoundland in 1638 or 1639 (the sources differ). France appointed a governor at Plaisance (Placentia) in 1655, so English and French settlements stood side by side until the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.

eras.polity: Newfoundland under Britain - the fishing colony
eras.note: By the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 France gave up its Newfoundland claims but kept fishing rights on the French Shore; a French force took St John's in 1762 and was beaten at Signal Hill, and the 1783 Treaty of Paris gave American fishermen fishing rights. Baptisms, marriages and burials of the period were recorded by the churches, whose originals generally stayed with them.

Britain recognised Newfoundland as a colony in 1824 (some sources say 1825), an elected House of Assembly followed in 1832, and a two-chamber legislature was restored in 1848. Responsible government was granted in 1854 and the first ministry took office in 1855.

Voters rejected Confederation with Canada in 1869 and again in 1895. Civil registration began in 1891, when clergy were required to register baptisms, marriages and burials with the government; before that the churches kept the only records, and in the 1940s they were asked to transcribe their older baptisms and marriages for the government. FamilySearch's Newfoundland vital records run 1840-1949 and include delayed registrations.

Dominion status dates from 26 September 1907, and full sovereignty from 15 November 1926 under the Balfour Declaration. In 1927 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council fixed the Labrador boundary in Newfoundland's favour.

The government voted itself out of existence in December 1933 and six commissioners were appointed on 16 February 1934. A referendum in June-July 1948 favoured joining Canada with 52.3 per cent, and union took effect in the last hours of 31 March 1949.

eras.polity: Canada - Province of Newfoundland (later Newfoundland and Labrador)
eras.note: Newfoundland became Canada's tenth province on 31 March 1949. The pre-1949 vital registrations remain the Newfoundland series (FamilySearch lists them for 1840-1949).

regions.label: Labrador and Quebec's Lower North Shore
regions.sub: Blanc-Sablon, Natashquan, North West River, Hebron, Nain, Cartwright

eras.polity: Labrador coast under the Newfoundland governor
eras.note: In 1763 Labrador was made a dependency of Newfoundland by royal proclamation, mainly to administer fishing rights, and was limited to a coastal strip.

eras.polity: Labrador coast under the Province of Quebec
eras.note: The Quebec Act of 1774 gave Quebec control of the territories assigned to Newfoundland in 1763, though Newfoundland kept regulating the fishery. Moravian missionaries, Hudson's Bay Company agents and settlers began working the central coast in the 1770s.
Newfoundland regained the territories it had lost in 1774 after lobbying in London.

eras.polity: Lower Canada, then Quebec, to Blanc-Sablon; Newfoundland's Labrador beyond
eras.note: An 1825 Act moved Lower Canada's border east to Blanc-Sablon and gave it territory up to the 52nd parallel, so the same coast was split between two jurisdictions. The Moravian mission at Hebron was established in 1831.

eras.polity: Labrador boundary fixed by the Privy Council
eras.note: On 1 March 1927 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council ruled for Newfoundland: the line runs north from Ance Sablon to the 52nd parallel, west to the Romaine River, north along the river and then along the watershed to Cape Chidley. The line was never marked on the ground and Quebec has never officially accepted it.

eras.polity: Canada - Quebec's Lower North Shore and Newfoundland and Labrador's Labrador
eras.note: The Newfoundland Act of 1949 specified Labrador's coast as delimited in 1927, turning the boundary into an internal provincial one. A family on this coast may have records in either Quebec or Newfoundland and Labrador depending on which side of the line the place lies.

regions.label: Southern Ontario - Upper Canada
regions.sub: Toronto (York), Kingston, Niagara, London, Hamilton, Windsor

eras.polity: French claim to the Great Lakes country
eras.note: France ceded its claim to Canada in the 1763 Treaty of Paris, ending French rule over this ground.

The Royal Proclamation of 7 October 1763 created the Province of Quebec; the Quebec Act of 1774 enlarged it to take in the Great Lakes country, and after 1783 Loyalist refugees arrived. The first townships (Royal and Cataraqui) were laid out along the St Lawrence and eastern Lake Ontario in 1784.

The Constitutional Act took effect on 26 December 1791, and Upper Canada was divided from Lower Canada. The capital was Newark (Niagara-on-the-Lake) from 1792 until it moved to York (Toronto) on 1 February 1796; district marriage registers at the Archives of Ontario run from 1801.

The Act of Union was proclaimed on 10 February 1841 and Upper Canada became Canada West. County marriage registers cover about 1858-1869; they do not hold every marriage, and births and deaths before 1869 are sparse.

Canada West became part of Ontario in 1867. Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths dates from 1 July 1869, though it was some years before it was widely followed; the Archives of Ontario holds the older registrations and the Office of the Registrar General the recent ones.

regions.label: Northern Ontario - Algoma to Hudson Bay
regions.sub: Sault Ste. Marie, Sudbury, Thunder Bay, Kenora, Moosonee, Manitoulin

eras.polity: Rupert's Land north of the divide
eras.note: The Hudson's Bay Company's 1670 charter gave it the Hudson Bay drainage basin, which takes in northern Ontario north of the Laurentian divide. France ceded its claim to Canada in 1763.

eras.polity: Rupert's Land (north) and the Province of Quebec / Upper Canada (south)
eras.note: North of the divide the Hudson's Bay Company ruled, and in 1821 it merged with the North West Company. South of it the ground followed the Southern Ontario sequence: Province of Quebec, Upper Canada from 1791, Canada West from 1841.

eras.polity: Province of Canada - Robinson Treaties and the new districts
eras.note: The Robinson Superior Treaty (7 September 1850) covered the north shore of Lake Superior and the Robinson Huron Treaty (9 September 1850) the north and east shores of Lake Huron. Algoma and Nipissing districts were set up in 1858 for judicial and administrative purposes.

eras.polity: Ontario south of the divide; Rupert's Land then the North-West Territories north of it
eras.note: At Confederation the part north of the Laurentian divide was still Rupert's Land; Ontario's boundaries were provisionally expanded in 1874, Thunder Bay District was created in 1871 from Algoma, and Treaty 3 was signed on 3 October 1873. The Judicial Committee ruled in 1884 that the Lake of the Woods region belonged to Ontario.

The Canada (Ontario Boundary) Act of 1889 confirmed Ontario's boundary and set its northern limit at the Albany River. Treaty 9 (the James Bay Treaty) was first signed on 6 November 1905 at Osnaburg and other posts.

eras.polity: Ontario to Hudson Bay - District of Patricia
eras.note: The Ontario Boundaries Extension Act of 1912 moved the area from the Albany River to Hudson Bay from the North-West Territories to Ontario, first as the District of Patricia (its merger into Kenora District is dated 1927 or 1937 depending on the source). Ontario's civil registration (from 1869) applies throughout.

regions.label: Manitoba and the Red River
regions.sub: Winnipeg, Selkirk, Portage la Prairie, Brandon, The Pas, Churchill

eras.note: The Hudson's Bay Company charter of 1670 covered the Hudson Bay drainage basin, which takes in most of Manitoba. The 49th parallel replaced the drainage divide as the southern border by the Convention of 1818.

Lord Selkirk received his grant in 1811 and the first settlers arrived in 1812. The Battle of Seven Oaks in 1816 killed the colony's governor and about twenty others, and Selkirk signed a treaty with the Cree, Assiniboine and Ojibwa in 1817.

eras.polity: District of Assiniboia - Hudson's Bay Company rule
eras.note: After the 1821 merger of the Hudson's Bay and North West companies, the Assiniboia Council governed the Red River settlement until 1870, with a company court from 1839. The Archives of Manitoba, which includes the Hudson's Bay Company Archives, holds Red River Settlement records, including Council of Assiniboia minutes for 1835-1870.

The Manitoba Act received royal assent on 12 May 1870 and Manitoba became a province on 15 July 1870, following the Red River uprising under Louis Riel. Treaties 1 and 2 were signed in August 1871 and Treaty 5 in September 1875.

Provincial registration of births, marriages and deaths is dated to 1882 in genealogy guides; the Vital Statistics Agency holds those records, with some incomplete pre-1882 church records, and the Archives of Manitoba holds a small collection of church records. Treaty 5 adhesions were taken in 1889 and Treaty 10 in 1906.

regions.label: Saskatchewan
regions.sub: Regina, Saskatoon, Prince Albert, Battleford, Cumberland House, Moose Jaw

eras.note: Henry Kelsey, the first known European to enter the province, travelled up the Saskatchewan River in 1690. French traders established Fort La Jonquiere in 1751 and Fort de la Corne in 1753.

eras.polity: Rupert's Land - Hudson's Bay Company posts
eras.note: Samuel Hearne founded Cumberland House in 1774, the Hudson's Bay Company's first permanent post here; the company merged with the North West Company in 1821. The Palliser and Hind expeditions explored the prairie in the late 1850s and early 1860s.

Canada acquired Hudson's Bay Company territories in 1870 and formed the North-West Territories; the Dominion Lands Act of 1872 opened homesteading, the North-West Mounted Police arrived in 1874, and Treaty 4 (1874) and Treaty 6 (1876) were signed. Homestead files from 1872 to 1930 are held by the Saskatchewan Archives.

The name Saskatchewan was adopted in 1882 for a provisional district of the North-West Territories. The Battle of Batoche in the 1885 North-West Rebellion followed, after which many Métis had already moved to the Prince Albert and South Branch areas. Genealogy guides date civil registration of births, marriages and deaths to 1895.
Saskatchewan became a province on 1 September 1905 (inaugurated 4 September), carved out of the North-West Territories. Treaty 10 (1906) covered the north-west of the province.

regions.label: Alberta
regions.sub: Edmonton, Calgary, Lethbridge, Fort Macleod, Red Deer, Fort Chipewyan

eras.polity: Rupert's Land - Hudson's Bay Company claim
eras.note: The Hudson's Bay Company claimed central and southern Alberta as part of Rupert's Land in 1670; Anthony Henday explored the Red Deer and Edmonton area in 1754-55, and Fort Chipewyan was founded in 1788 (Fort Vermilion also claims 1788). The company merged with the North West Company in 1821.

eras.polity: Rupert's Land - Hudson's Bay Company and the missions
eras.note: Missionaries came in the 1840s: Jean-Baptiste Thibault reached Lac Sainte Anne in 1842 and Robert Rundle established Rundle's Mission in 1847.
The land became part of the North-West Territories on 15 July 1870. The North-West Mounted Police marched west in July 1874, and Treaty 6 (1876) and Treaty 7 (22 September 1877) were signed.

The District of Alberta was created in 1882. Treaty 8 was signed on 8 July 1899. Registration of vital events is usually dated to 1898, though earlier start dates are also quoted; the Provincial Archives of Alberta holds the registrations and indexes.
Alberta became a province on 1 September 1905. Records of the North-West Territories period before 1905 are federal and held at Library and Archives Canada.

regions.label: British Columbia
regions.sub: Barkerville, Kamloops, Prince George, Prince Rupert, Williams Lake, Atlin

eras.polity: Fur-trade coast - Hudson's Bay Company districts
eras.note: Captain James Cook reached Nootka Sound in 1778 and the Nootka Conventions of 1793-94 gave Britain sovereignty over Vancouver Island and nearby islands. The Hudson's Bay Company began Fort Victoria in 1843, and the Oregon Treaty of 1846 set the border at the 49th parallel, swinging south to keep the island British.

Vancouver Island was granted to the Hudson's Bay Company by Letters Patent on 13 January 1849 and made a Crown colony; the company leased it from 1849 to 1859. The mainland remained fur-trading districts run by the company.

eras.polity: Colony of British Columbia (mainland) and Colony of Vancouver Island
eras.note: The mainland colony was created in 1858 in response to the Fraser Canyon gold rush, with New Westminster as capital under Richard Clement Moody of the Royal Engineers. James Douglas governed both colonies from 1858, and the Vancouver Island Assembly had met since 1855.
The Act uniting the two colonies took effect on 6 August 1866 (one source dates the merged colony to November 1866). The united colony joined Canadian Confederation in 1871.

The Births, Deaths and Marriages Act of 1872 began provincial registration; it excluded Chinese and Indigenous people, a clause removed in 1888, and amendments in 1897 and 1899 changed the position for Indigenous people again. The BC Archives also searches baptisms (1836-1901) and colonial marriages (1859-1872) outside the registration series; the baptism registers themselves stay with the BC Vital Statistics Agency.

regions.label: Yukon and the Northwest Territories
regions.sub: Dawson City, Whitehorse, Fort Selkirk, Fort Simpson, Yellowknife

eras.note: In December 1821 the company's monopoly was extended to the Pacific coast. Company traders set up posts in the 1840s: Lapierre House in 1846, Fort Yukon in 1847 and Fort Selkirk in 1848 (sacked in 1852 and not rebuilt until 1889).

The United Kingdom transferred the North-Western Territory to Canada in 1870. Fort Reliance was established in 1874, and paying gold was found on the Stewart River in 1885 and on the Fortymile River in 1886.

The Yukon District was carved out of the North-West Territories in 1895. Gold discovered on Bonanza Creek on 16 August 1896 began the Klondike Gold Rush, and Dawson City grew to about 17,000 people by summer 1898.

eras.polity: Yukon Territory (capital Dawson); Northwest Territories east of it
eras.note: The Yukon became its own territory on 13 June 1898 with the Yukon Act, and the 1901 census counted 27,219 people. Treaty 11 was signed between 27 June and 22 August 1921 in the Northwest Territories.

The Yukon capital moved from Dawson City to Whitehorse on 1 April 1953, and responsible government came to the Yukon in October 1979. The Umbrella Final Agreement on First Nations land claims was signed in 1992.

regions.label: New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory
regions.sub: Sydney, Newcastle, Dubbo, Tamworth, Canberra

eras.polity: Colony of New South Wales - the first British settlement
eras.note: The First Fleet reached Sydney Cove on 25 January 1788 and the colony was proclaimed on 7 February 1788. At its greatest extent it took in Queensland, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia, the Northern Territory and New Zealand. From 1788 to 1856 the only records of births, marriages and burials were the registers kept by the churches.

eras.polity: Colony of New South Wales - church registers only
eras.note: The Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages holds transcribed volumes of church records, not the originals, which are with the State Archives Collection of the NSW Museums of History. It took over 1834-1855 baptisms, marriages and burials of non-Anglican denominations from the Supreme Court in 1856 and, under an Act of 1879, copies of the Church of England registers for 1825-1855.

eras.polity: Colony of New South Wales - civil registration and responsible government
eras.note: Compulsory civil registration began on 1 March 1856 under an Act of that year, and responsible government followed on 6 June 1856. The Registry's index covers registrations and the early church records together, with entries back to 1787.

eras.polity: Australia - State of New South Wales
eras.note: Federation took effect on 1 January 1901 and the colony became a state of the Commonwealth.

eras.polity: Australia - State of New South Wales; Australian Capital Territory from 1911
eras.note: New South Wales transferred the Australian Capital Territory to the Commonwealth on 1 January 1911, so events there after that date lie outside the state. Canberra was named as the capital in March 1913 (12 or 20 March depending on the source).

regions.label: Victoria - the Port Phillip District
regions.sub: Melbourne, Geelong, Ballarat, Portland, Hamilton, Lilydale

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Port Phillip District of New South Wales
eras.note: The district was part of New South Wales from 9 September 1836 until 1 July 1851. Its northern boundary was redefined several times before the 1842 Australian Constitutions Act set it on the Murray. Births, Deaths and Marriages Victoria now holds the early church records for the district, dated from 1836 or 1837 depending on the source, to 1853.

eras.polity: Colony of Victoria - church registers still the only record
eras.note: Victoria separated from New South Wales on 1 July 1851. Gold was found the same year (the first marketable find was at Clunes on 1 July 1851) and the population grew from about 75,000 in 1851 to about 500,000 in 1861.

The Registration (Births, Deaths and Marriages) Act was proclaimed on 18 January 1853 and registration with a District Registrar became compulsory on 1 July 1853. The registry's own history and the Public Record Office Victoria differ on whether its church records begin in 1836 or 1837.
Federation took effect on 1 January 1901. The present Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages was formally established under the 1985 Act.

regions.label: Tasmania - Van Diemen's Land
regions.sub: Hobart, Launceston, Sorell, Campbell Town, Deloraine, King Island

eras.polity: Van Diemen's Land - a dependency of New South Wales
eras.note: A military outpost was set up at Risdon Cove on the eastern shore of the Derwent in August 1803, and Hobart Town was founded at Sullivans Cove in 1804. Libraries Tasmania lists marriages from 1803 and an index to baptisms from 1803.

eras.polity: Van Diemen's Land - a separate convict colony
eras.note: It became a separate colony on 3 December 1825. About 73,000 convicts were transported to Van Diemen's Land, roughly 40% of all those sent to Australia, until transportation ended in 1853. Civil registration is dated 1838 or 1839 depending on the source, and Libraries Tasmania lists district registers from 1839.
Libraries Tasmania lists a register of convicts' deaths for 1840-1874. The 1851 census counted 70,130 people, 24.3% of them convicts.

The name changed from Van Diemen's Land to Tasmania on 1 January 1856, so records before then are filed under the old name. Self-government is dated 1855 or 1856 depending on the source, and the last penal settlement, Port Arthur, closed permanently in 1877.
Federation took effect on 1 January 1901.

regions.label: South Australia
regions.sub: Adelaide, Port Pirie, Kangaroo Island, Port Lincoln, Mount Gambier

eras.note: Before registers.

An Act of Parliament of 15 August 1834 established the province and Governor Hindmarsh proclaimed it at Glenelg on 28 December 1836. It was founded without convict labour, and Old Lutherans from Brandenburg arrived from 1838.

eras.polity: Province of South Australia - civil registration
eras.note: Civil registration began in 1842, earlier than in Victoria (1853) or New South Wales (1856).

South Australia became a self-governing colony in October 1856 under the Constitution Act 1856. The Northern Territory was transferred to South Australia in 1863 and stayed with it until 1 January 1911.
Federation took effect on 1 January 1901.

regions.label: Western Australia - the Swan River Colony
regions.sub: Perth, Fremantle, Albany, Esperance, Kalgoorlie

eras.note: Before registers.
A military garrison was established at King George Sound on 26 December 1826 under Major Edmund Lockyer.

eras.polity: Swan River Colony, renamed Western Australia in 1832
eras.note: The colony's founding is dated 17 June 1829 in one source and 12 August 1829 in another. It was renamed the Colony of Western Australia on 6 February 1832, though Swan River Colony stayed in informal use. Civil registration began in 1841.

eras.polity: Colony of Western Australia - penal colony
eras.note: Western Australia became a penal colony in 1850 and over 9,000 convicts had been transported by 1868. It gained self-government in 1890.
Western Australia joined the Commonwealth as a state on 1 January 1901.

regions.label: Northern Territory
regions.sub: Darwin, Katherine, Alice Springs, Arnhem Land

eras.note: Before registers. Indigenous peoples have lived here for at least 48,400 to 68,700 years, and Sulawesi traders collected trepang with them from the 17th or 18th century.

The area became part of New South Wales in 1825 and was briefly part of the colony of North Australia between February and December 1846. British attempts to settle the coast failed in 1824-1828, 1838-1849 and 1864-1866.
The Territory was transferred to South Australia in 1863. A settlement at Port Darwin succeeded in 1869, and civil registration is dated 1870.

eras.polity: Australia - Northern Territory under federal control
eras.note: The Territory was separated from South Australia and transferred to federal control on 1 January 1911. Darwin was bombed on 19 February 1942, and most of the Top End was under military government during the war.
Self-government began on 1 July 1978 under the Northern Territory (Self-Government) Act 1978. The Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act began operating in January 1977.

regions.label: New Zealand - the North Island
regions.sub: Auckland, Wellington, Rotorua, Napier, Gisborne

eras.polity: Maori iwi and hapu; European contact
eras.note: Before registers. Abel Tasman reached New Zealand on 13 December 1642 and James Cook in October 1769. Polynesian settlement is dated to roughly 1320-1350 CE.

eras.polity: British sovereignty proclaimed; a dependency of New South Wales
eras.note: The Treaty of Waitangi was signed on 6 February 1840 and William Hobson proclaimed sovereignty on 21 May 1840. Letters patent of 15 June 1839 had extended New South Wales to include New Zealand.
The colony became separate from New South Wales on 3 May 1841. Registration of births and deaths began in 1848 under the Colonial Secretary's Office, and marriage registration followed in 1854.

eras.polity: Colony of New Zealand - the provinces
eras.note: The provinces were created under the 1852 Constitution Act and came into being on 17 January 1853. On this island they were Auckland, New Plymouth (renamed Taranaki on 1 January 1859), Wellington and Hawke's Bay (split from Wellington on 1 November 1858), and they were abolished in 1876.
Birth registrations began to record parents' ages and birthplaces and details of marriage in 1875, and marriage registrations began to include parental details and residence in October 1880.

eras.polity: Dominion, then Realm, of New Zealand
eras.note: Separate registers for Maori marriages were introduced in 1911 and for Maori births and deaths in 1913. Maori marriages were merged into the general register in 1952 and Maori births and deaths in 1962.

regions.label: New Zealand - the South Island
regions.sub: Christchurch, Dunedin, Nelson, Invercargill, Greymouth

eras.polity: Maori iwi and hapu; European contact
eras.note: Before registers. Abel Tasman first reached New Zealand on 13 December 1642.

eras.polity: British sovereignty by discovery; a dependency of New South Wales
eras.note: William Hobson based Britain's claim to the South and Stewart Islands on discovery, and to the North Island on the Treaty of Waitangi, in a proclamation of 21 May 1840.
The colony separated from New South Wales on 3 May 1841. The BDM historical index of the Department of Internal Affairs runs from 1848 for births and deaths and from 1854 for marriages.

eras.polity: Colony of New Zealand - the provinces
eras.note: The South Island provinces were Nelson, Canterbury and Otago, with Marlborough split from Nelson on 1 November 1859, Southland from Otago in 1861 (reunited in 1870) and Westland from Canterbury on 1 December 1873.
