The Canterbury Provincial Government archives for 1853-1877, about 35,000 listed items including goldfields and Ngai Tahu material, are held at Archives New Zealand in Christchurch.
Gold was found at Gabriel's Gully in Central Otago in 1861 and in Westland in 1865. The provinces were abolished in 1876.

eras.polity: Dominion, then Realm, of New Zealand
eras.note: New Zealand became a self-governing Dominion in 1907.

regions.label: Cook Islands - Rarotonga and the Southern Group
regions.sub: Avarua, Arorangi, Rarotonga, Aitutaki, Mangaia

eras.note: Before registers. Polynesian settlement is dated to about AD 1000, Alvaro de Mendana sighted Pukapuka in 1595, and James Cook visited in 1773 and 1777.

eras.polity: Island chiefdoms and the London Missionary Society
eras.note: English missionaries arrived in 1821. The Pacific Manuscripts Bureau catalogues the archives of the Cook Islands Christian Church (MS 1410), including London Missionary Society birth records and Avarua baptism and burial books.
The islands became a British protectorate in 1888 after a petition from Queen Makea Takau Ariki. Seven instruments of cession were signed on 8 and 9 October 1900.

eras.polity: Part of the Colony, then Dominion, of New Zealand
eras.note: The islands were included in the Colony of New Zealand by Order in Council effective 11 June 1901. FamilySearch indexes Cook Islands civil registers for 1846-2022, with the originals held by the Ministry of Justice, Rarotonga, and the Land and Survey Office, Avarua.

eras.polity: Self-governing in free association with New Zealand
eras.note: A constitution promulgated on 4 August 1965 established self-government in free association with New Zealand.

regions.label: Guam
regions.sub: Hagatna, Dededo, Agat, Yigo, Humatak

eras.note: Before registers. Magellan's fleet arrived on 6 March 1521 and Spain formally claimed Guam in 1565.

eras.polity: Spanish Mariana Islands - the Jesuit mission
eras.note: The galleon San Diego arrived on 15 June 1668 with Jesuit missionaries led by Diego Luis de San Vitores. The Spanish-Chamorro wars ran from 1670 to 1683.

eras.polity: Spanish Mariana Islands - the Augustinian Recollects
eras.note: The Jesuits were expelled from the Marianas in 1769 and succeeded by the Augustinian Recollects. The parish of Dulce Nombre de Maria at Hagatna recorded a chronicle for 1846-1899, and FamilySearch holds images of the 1897 Guam census, with originals at the Micronesian Area Research Center, University of Guam.

US forces captured Guam on 21 June 1898 and the Treaty of Paris ceded it. FamilySearch's Guam collection holds images of court records for 1901-1935 and land records for 1896-1902, with originals at the Micronesian Area Research Center.
Japan invaded Guam on 8 December 1941, American troops landed on 21 July 1944 and Japanese forces officially surrendered on 10 August 1944.
A civilian government was established for the first time by the Guam Organic Act in 1950.

eras.polity: Guam - unincorporated territory of the United States
eras.note: FamilySearch's Guam collection includes indexed obituaries, dated 1970-1999 in its contents list and 1970-2000 in its introduction.

regions.label: Northern Luzon: Ilocos, Cagayan Valley, the Cordillera and Batanes
regions.sub: Vigan, Laoag, Tuguegarao, Bangued, Bayombong, Basco

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: province of Ilocos, bishopric of Nueva Segovia
eras.note: Juan de Salcedo reached Vigan on 13 June 1572 and founded Villa Fernandina de Vigan, the seat of the diocese of Nueva Segovia; in 1574 he received the province of Ylocos as an encomienda, which took in parts of present-day Abra and Mountain Province. The islands were governed from Mexico City as part of the Viceroyalty of New Spain until 1821, and Spanish central-government papers on the Philippines are held in the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, which PARES searches.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, and Batanes under Cagayan
eras.note: Ilocos was divided into Ilocos Norte and Ilocos Sur on 2 February 1818, so a register before and after that date may be catalogued under different province names. Spain claimed the Batanes islands in 1783 under Governor-General Jose Basco y Vargas, and they were ruled as part of Cagayan province.

eras.polity: United States: Insular Government, then the Commonwealth
eras.note: The Treaty of Paris of 10 December 1898 ceded the Philippines to the United States; American civil government was introduced in Ilocos in 1901-1902, and the Philippine-American War officially ended in 1902. Batanes was made a sub-province of Cagayan on 20 August 1907 (Act No. 1693) and an independent province on 20 May 1909 (Act No. 1952).
Japanese forces landed on Batanes on 8 December 1941. From 1942 to 1944 the province was reduced to a municipality of Cagayan, and the islands were liberated in early 1945.

The United States recognised Philippine independence on 4 July 1946. Abra, Mountain Province and Benguet were moved to the new Cordillera Administrative Region on 15 July 1987 (Executive Order No. 220), so a regional search may not match the older Ilocos or Cagayan groupings.

regions.label: Central Luzon and Pangasinan: Lingayen to Bataan
regions.sub: Lingayen, Dagupan, Tarlac, San Fernando, Cabanatuan, Malolos, Iba

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Pampanga, the first Spanish province on Luzon, and the district of Pangasinan
eras.note: Pampanga was organised as a province on 11 December 1571 and at first covered almost all of Central Luzon, including parts of today's Tarlac, Bataan, Zambales, Nueva Ecija and Bulacan. Martin de Goiti began the conquest of Pangasinan in 1571-1573, and it became a district with Lingayen as its capital on 5 April 1580.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Bataan, Bulacan, Nueva Ecija and Tarlac carved from Pampanga
eras.note: Bataan was created in 1754 from eight Pampanga municipalities. In 1848 towns passed from Pampanga to Nueva Ecija and Bulacan, and Tarlac was formed in 1873 from five northern towns that had been under a military command since 1860; Pampanga's present borders date from 1873, so a town's register may sit under a former province. Bacolor was the provisional Spanish capital during the British occupation of Manila in 1762-1764.

eras.polity: United States rule; the Malolos republic of 1899
eras.note: Aguinaldo established the First Philippine Republic at Malolos on 23 January 1899, and the Philippine-American War began on 4 February 1899; the war is officially dated to end on 16 April 1902, when General Miguel Malvar surrendered. American civil government began on 1 July 1901.
Japan invaded on 8 December 1941 and the first troops landed in northern Luzon on 10 December. The Allied liberation campaign ran from 20 October 1944 to 15 August 1945.

eras.polity: Philippines: Pangasinan in Region I from 1973
eras.note: Presidential Decree No. 1 of 1973 transferred Pangasinan from Region III to Region I, so Pangasinan may be listed under the Ilocos regional heading rather than Central Luzon.

regions.label: Manila, Southern Tagalog and Bicol
regions.sub: Manila, Cavite, Calamba, Batangas, Lucena, Naga, Legazpi

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Manila the capital, under New Spain
eras.note: Martin de Goiti conquered Maynila in 1570 and Legazpi renamed it Nueva Castilla and made it the capital. The Spanish first landed in Bicol in 1567 at Gibal-ong in Sorsogon, and Bicol shipyards built Manila galleons. The Philippines was governed from Mexico City as part of the Viceroyalty of New Spain until 1821.
Archbishop Rojo signed the surrender of Manila on 30 October 1762. The Treaty of Paris of 10 February 1763, which ended the Seven Years' War, returned the Philippines to Spain.
A census of 1818 recorded Spanish-Filipino families in several provinces, among them Albay (1,311) and Camarines Norte (1,810).

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: surnames by decree, civil registers from 1888
eras.note: Governor-General Narciso Claveria's decree of 21 November 1849 had a catalogue of 61,000 surnames sent to provincial heads, each surname going to one family per municipality; a Spanish surname therefore does not show Spanish ancestry. The catalogue (Catalogo alfabetico de apellidos) was reprinted by the National Archives in 1973. FamilySearch's local civil registration collection begins in 1888, coverage varies by locality, and Metro Manila has a separate collection.

eras.polity: United States: Insular Government, then the Commonwealth
eras.note: American forces took Manila on 13 August 1898 and the Treaty of Paris of 10 December 1898 ceded the islands; civil government under William Howard Taft began on 1 July 1901. Act No. 3753 of 1930, the Civil Registry Law, set up a national civil register with the Director of the National Library as Civil Registrar-General and took effect in 1931.

eras.polity: Japanese occupation; the Second Philippine Republic
eras.note: Manila was occupied on 2 January 1942 and the Japanese-sponsored Second Philippine Republic was proclaimed on 14 October 1943. The Battle of Manila ran from 3 February to 3 March 1945.

FamilySearch dates its local civil registration collection 1888-1986 (the description also says 1984), with the originals given as held by the Bureau of Records Management in Manila and the National Statistics Office.

regions.label: The Visayas: Cebu, Panay, Negros, Bohol, Leyte and Samar
regions.sub: Cebu, Iloilo, Dumaguete, Tagbilaran, Tacloban, Borongan

eras.note: Before registers. Ruy Lopez de Villalobos reached Leyte and Samar in 1543 and named the islands Las Islas Filipinas after Prince Philip.
Legazpi's expedition arrived off Cebu on 13 February 1565 and conquered it; in 1569 he moved to Panay and founded a second settlement. The Crown permitted the encomienda system in 1568.
After 1821 the islands were administered from Madrid, and Philippine ports were opened to world trade in 1834.

eras.polity: United States: military government, then the Insular Government
eras.note: Military government began on 14 August 1898 and its office ended in July 1902; the Philippine Organic Act dates from July 1902, and the Commonwealth was inaugurated on 15 November 1935.
The Allied liberation campaign ran from 20 October 1944 to 15 August 1945, and Japan surrendered on 2 September 1945.
The United States recognised Philippine independence on 4 July 1946.

regions.label: Mindanao and the Sulu archipelago
regions.sub: Davao, Cagayan de Oro, Zamboanga, Butuan, General Santos, Jolo

eras.note: Before registers. The Sultanate of Sulu is dated to 17 November 1405 or to about 1457, depending on the source.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines beside the Sultanate of Sulu
eras.note: The Spanish-Moro conflict is dated 1565-1898. The Sultanate of Sulu became independent of Brunei in 1578; the Dutch attacked Zamboanga and made an expedition to Jolo in 1648. Spain attacked Balanguingui in 1848 and Jolo in 1851, and a peace treaty of 30 April 1851 was read differently by the two sides.
Spain captured Jolo in 1876.

eras.polity: United States: military government and the Moro Rebellion
eras.note: The Treaty of Paris of 10 December 1898 ceded the Philippines to the United States; the Moro Rebellion is dated 1902-1913.
Moro Province was created on 1 June 1903 under Act No. 787 and abolished on 23 July 1914.

eras.polity: United States: Department of Mindanao and Sulu
eras.note: The Department of Mindanao and Sulu replaced Moro Province on 23 July 1914. Under the Carpenter Agreement of 22 March 1915 the sultan of Sulu gave up sovereignty over United States-controlled territory and kept religious authority only.
Japan invaded the Philippines on 8 December 1941 and surrendered on 2 September 1945.
The United States recognised Philippine independence on 4 July 1946.

regions.label: Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and Himachal
regions.sub: Delhi, Amritsar, Ambala, Panipat, Shimla, Chandigarh

eras.polity: Mughal Empire: Delhi and Lahore subahs
eras.note: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, founding the Mughal Empire. The empire was divided into provinces (subahs), split into sarkars and then parganas. Nader Shah of Iran sacked Delhi in 1739.

eras.polity: Successor powers: Sikh Empire in the Punjab; Delhi under the Marathas, then the Company's protection
eras.note: Mahadaji Shinde restored Maratha control over northern India, including Delhi, and after the Marathas lost influence the East India Company became protector of the Mughal dynasty at Delhi. The Company defeated the Sikh Empire at the Battle of Gujrat on 21 February 1849.

The Punjab was annexed on 29 March 1849 (29 March or 2 April depending on the source) and run by a three-member Board of Administration under the Bengal Presidency; a Chief Commissioner replaced the board in 1853. The last Mughal emperor was deposed in September 1857 after the Siege of Delhi.

eras.polity: British Raj: Punjab under a Lieutenant-Governor
eras.note: After the Crown took direct control in 1858 the Delhi Territory was transferred to the Punjab, which became a Lieutenant-Governor's province (1858 or 1859, depending on the passage). The North-West Frontier Province was separated from the Punjab in 1901.

eras.polity: British Raj: Delhi separate, Punjab a Governor's province
eras.note: Delhi District was separated from the Punjab in 1911, and the Punjab became a Governor's province in 1921. Registers of Europeans and Eurasian Christians are indexed by FIBIS, and Findmypast's British India Office marriages use transcriptions licensed from FIBIS.

eras.polity: India: East Punjab and Delhi after partition
eras.note: The Punjab was partitioned in 1947 into East Punjab (India) and West Punjab (Pakistan), with Bengal and Punjab divided along district-level religious majorities; the provincial capital, Lahore, went to West Punjab. The two dominions legally came into existence at midnight on 14-15 August 1947.

regions.label: Uttar Pradesh: Agra, Awadh, Rohilkhand and the Doab
regions.sub: Agra, Mathura, Kanpur, Prayagraj, Lucknow, Varanasi, Gorakhpur

eras.note: The Mughal Empire dates from 1526. Aurangzeb ruled from 1658 until his death in 1707, after which succession disputes and the rise of the Marathas weakened central authority.

eras.polity: Awadh and the successor states of the Mughal Empire
eras.note: Nader Shah's sack of Delhi in 1739 was followed by the breakaway of many provincial elites. The East India Company received revenue rights in Bengal by the Treaty of Allahabad of 16 August 1765.

eras.polity: East India Company: Ceded and Conquered Provinces, North-Western Provinces, Oudh
eras.note: Rohilkhand, the lower Doab and the Gorakhpur division were ceded in 1801, and a statute of 1835 authorised a lieutenant-governor for the North-Western Provinces. Awadh (Oudh) was annexed in 1856, and the Rebellion of 1857 ran from 10 May 1857 into 1858.

eras.polity: British Raj: North-Western Provinces and Oudh
eras.note: Crown rule began on 1 November 1858. The offices of Lieutenant-Governor and Chief Commissioner were combined in 1877.

eras.polity: British Raj: United Provinces of Agra and Oudh
eras.note: The name United Provinces of Agra and Oudh came into use in 1902. Allahabad was the administrative headquarters, and Lucknow became the capital some time after 1921.
The province was renamed Uttar Pradesh when the Constitution took effect on 26 January 1950.

regions.label: Bengal, Bihar, Jharkhand and Odisha: the Bengal Presidency
regions.sub: Kolkata, Patna, Cuttack, Ranchi, Bokaro, Deoghar

eras.note: Company trading posts in the Mughal Bengal Subah date from 1612.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Bengal Presidency
eras.note: The Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal at Plassey on 23 June 1757 and at Buxar in 1764, and received revenue rights in 1765. The Permanent Settlement of 1793 fixed the land tax; territories such as the North-Western Provinces, Punjab, Burma and Assam were later separated from the presidency. Calcutta was India's capital until 1911.

Registration of births and deaths began in Calcutta in 1864 but was generally voluntary. The Anglican baptism, marriage and burial returns sent to London are in the British Library's India Office Records, Bengal series N/1 (dated 1713-1947 in the catalogue), with FIBIS indexes.

eras.polity: British Raj: Bengal partitioned, Eastern Bengal and Assam
eras.note: The partition of Bengal in 1905 created Eastern Bengal and Assam; the arrangement was reversed in 1912.

eras.polity: British Raj: Bihar and Orissa Province, with Bengal
eras.note: Bihar and Orissa was separated from the Bengal Presidency in 1912, on 22 March or 1 April depending on the passage, with Patna as capital.

eras.polity: British Raj: Bengal, Bihar and Orissa as separate provinces
eras.note: On 1 April 1936 Bihar and Orissa was divided into Bihar Province (including present-day Jharkhand) and Orissa Province. The Bengal Presidency, called the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal until 1937, became the Bengal Province.

eras.polity: India: West Bengal, Bihar and Odisha
eras.note: Bengal was divided in 1947 into East Bengal and West Bengal. French Chandernagore was ceded to India on 2 May 1950 and merged with West Bengal on 2 October 1954.

regions.label: Central India: Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and the Nagpur country
regions.sub: Bhopal, Jabalpur, Sagar, Ujjain, Raipur, Nagpur

eras.note: The Mughal Empire dates from 1526; under Aurangzeb (1658-1707) it reached its greatest extent, and his Deccan campaigns weakened governance.

eras.polity: Maratha confederacy: Scindia, Holkar and the Bhonsle of Nagpur
eras.note: After the Third Battle of Panipat on 14 January 1761 the Maratha state was led by a confederacy of leading families: Scindia, Holkar, Bhonsle and Gaekwad. The transition from Mughal to Maratha control was gradual and varied by place. The Third Anglo-Maratha War ended Maratha independence in 1817-1818, and Nagpur's Maratha rulers submitted to British sovereignty in 1818.

eras.polity: East India Company: Saugor and Nerbudda Territories, Nagpur
eras.note: The Saugor and Nerbudda Territories were formed in 1820 from Maratha cessions of 1817-1818. Nagpur was annexed in 1853 after Raghoji III died without heirs, under the doctrine of lapse.

eras.polity: British Raj: Central Provinces, later Central Provinces and Berar
eras.note: The Central Provinces were created in 1861 from the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories and Nagpur Province, and were renamed Central Provinces and Berar on 24 October 1936.

eras.polity: India: Central Provinces and Berar, Madhya Bharat, Vindhya Pradesh, Bhopal
eras.note: On the Constitution's coming into force in 1950 the province was reorganised as Madhya Pradesh; Madhya Bharat, Vindhya Pradesh and Bhopal remained separate states until 1956.
On 1 November 1956 Madhya Bharat, Vindhya Pradesh and Bhopal were merged into Madhya Pradesh.
Chhattisgarh was split off from Madhya Pradesh in 2000.

regions.label: Rajasthan and Gujarat: Rajputana, Baroda, Kathiawar and Kutch
regions.sub: Jaipur, Ajmer, Mount Abu, Rajkot, Anand, Bhavnagar, Gandhidham

eras.polity: Mughal Empire, with Rajput states under its suzerainty
eras.note: Most Rajput rulers accepted Mughal suzerainty under Akbar, though Mewar and Marwar refused.

eras.polity: Maratha confederacy and the Rajput states
eras.note: Rajputana came under Maratha influence as the Mughal Empire declined in the late 18th century, and the Gaekwad family of the Maratha confederacy ruled Baroda. The British replaced the Marathas as overlords in 1818.

eras.polity: East India Company: Rajputana Agency and the Bombay Presidency
eras.note: Treaties were made with the Rajput states after the Pindari war, from 1817, and by the end of 1818 similar treaties covered the rest. The Rajputana Agency was established at Ajmer in 1832 and its headquarters moved to Mount Abu in 1845.

eras.polity: British Raj: Rajputana Agency, Ajmer-Merwara and the Bombay Presidency
eras.note: Rajputana comprised nineteen princely states, three chiefships and the British district of Ajmer-Merwara, which was under direct British rule. The Bombay Presidency came under direct Crown rule after 1858-1859.

eras.polity: India: Rajasthan, Bombay State, Saurashtra and Kutch
eras.note: Rajasthan was formed on 30 March 1949 from the states of the Rajputana Agency. Bombay State, formed in 1950, included Baroda and the Dangs.

eras.polity: India: the enlarged bilingual Bombay State
eras.note: Under the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 Bombay State absorbed Saurashtra and Kutch.
Bombay State was split on 1 May 1960 into Maharashtra and Gujarat.

regions.label: Maharashtra: Konkan, the Deccan, Marathwada and Berar
regions.sub: Mumbai, Pune, Nashik, Kolhapur, Akola, Nanded

eras.polity: The Deccan before the Maratha state
eras.note: Before registers. Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati on 6 June 1674.

eras.polity: Maratha Empire: the Chhatrapati at Satara, the Peshwa at Pune
eras.note: Balaji Vishwanath was appointed Peshwa in 1713; the Peshwa's seat was Poona from 1728 to 1818 and the Chhatrapati's was Satara from 1700. Bombay itself was ceded by Portugal to England in 1661 and taken over by the East India Company in 1668. The Third Anglo-Maratha War ended in 1818, with Pune coming under direct British rule while Satara and Kolhapur kept local Maratha rulers.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Bombay Presidency
eras.note: The Peshwa's dominions were annexed to the Bombay Presidency in stages up to 1818. The British Library's India Office Records hold the Bombay Anglican returns as series N/3 (dated 1709-1947 in the catalogue).

eras.polity: British Raj: Bombay Presidency, Berar and Hyderabad
eras.note: Berar was leased to the British on 5 November 1902, merged on 17 September 1903 and placed under the Central Provinces commissioner from 1 October 1903, although it remained under nominal Hyderabad sovereignty until the Central Provinces and Berar were formed on 24 October 1936.
The province became Bombay State in 1947 and a Part-A state in 1950.

eras.polity: India: the enlarged bilingual Bombay State
eras.note: The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 gave Bombay State Marathwada and Vidarbha, and sent Belgaum, Bijapur, Dharwar and North Canara to Mysore State.
Maharashtra was formed on 1 May 1960 with Bombay as its capital.

regions.label: Goa: the Estado da India
regions.sub: Panaji, Old Goa, Margao, Mapusa, Vasco da Gama

eras.note: Before registers. Goa was held by the Bijapur Sultanate when Afonso de Albuquerque captured it in 1510.

eras.polity: Portuguese India: Goa the capital of the Estado da India
eras.note: The Estado da India capital moved from Cochin to Velha Goa in 1530, the Goa Inquisition was established in 1560, and by the end of the 17th century fewer than 10 percent of Goa's population was non-Christian. The Historical Archives of Goa at Panaji hold baptism and other registers, and the LDS Church microfilmed parish records from 146 locations in Goa, many of them unindexed.

eras.polity: Portuguese India: Nova Goa (Panjim) the capital
eras.note: The capital moved to Nova Goa (Panjim) in 1843. Portugal lost Dadra and Nagar Haveli in 1954, and FamilySearch catalogues Panaji parish register copies for 1913-1996.
India annexed Goa in December 1961; the Portuguese governor signed the Instrument of Surrender on 19 December 1961.
Portugal recognised Indian sovereignty in a treaty signed on 31 December 1974, and Goa became an Indian state on 30 May 1987.

regions.label: South India: Madras, Mysore, Kerala and the Carnatic
regions.sub: Chennai, Pondicherry, Bengaluru, Mysore, Kochi, Madurai

eras.polity: South Indian kingdoms; Portuguese coastal bases from 1505
eras.note: Before registers. The Portuguese Estado da India was founded in 1505, with bases on the Malabar Coast; its capital was at Cochin until 1530.

eras.polity: East India Company: Fort St George; French Pondichery
eras.note: The Company bought Madraspatnam in 1639-1640 and set up the Agency of Fort St George; it was made a presidency again in 1684, and the French held Madras from 1746 to 1749. Pondichery was French from 1673 (the Dutch held it 1693-1699) and was returned to France in 1765 after the Treaty of Paris of 1763. Madras became one of three Company presidencies in 1785.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Madras Presidency
eras.note: The Carnatic Treaty of 1801 brought the Carnatic under British rule, and the Presidency took over the administration of the Kingdom of Mysore in 1831; Mysore was restored in 1881. The Anglican returns of the presidency are in the British Library's India Office Records as series N/2 (dated 1698-1947 in the catalogue).

eras.polity: British Raj: Madras Presidency, Mysore and the French establishments
eras.note: Madras came under direct Crown rule in 1858, the French establishments were returned to France on 26 September 1816, and the presidency became the Province of Madras in 1937.

eras.polity: India: Madras State and Mysore State
eras.note: The Province of Madras became Madras State on 26 January 1950. Pondichery, Yanam, Mahe and Karikal were transferred de facto to India on 1 November 1954; France ratified the treaty in 1962.
Mysore State was formed on 1 November 1956 by adding areas of the former Bombay, Madras and Hyderabad States and Coorg, and was renamed Karnataka on 1 November 1973.

regions.label: Matabeleland and the western Midlands
regions.sub: Bulawayo, Gwanda, Hwange, Gweru, Kwekwe, Beitbridge

eras.note: Mzilikazi Khumalo led Nguni and other groups into the area of the Rozvi state in the late 1830s; 1840 is given as the founding of Matabeleland. The Rudd Concession of 1888 gave Cecil Rhodes mineral rights.

eras.polity: British South Africa Company rule (Southern Rhodesia from 1898)
eras.note: The First Matabele War ran 1893-94 (decisive battle 1 November 1893; Lobengula died in January 1894) and the Second Matabele War 1896-97. The name Southern Rhodesia was made official by Order in Council on 20 October 1898. The National Archives of Zimbabwe, in Harare, hold the archives of the former Southern Rhodesia.

A referendum on 27 October 1922 chose responsible government; the UK annexed Southern Rhodesia on 12 September 1923 and the first constitution took effect on 1 October 1923. The National Archives of Zimbabwe were established in 1935.

eras.polity: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, then Southern Rhodesia again
eras.note: The Federation's end is dated 1963 or 1 January 1964 depending on the source. From 1953 to 1963 the National Archives in Harare served as the central repository for the National Archives of Rhodesia and Nyasaland.

UDI was declared on 11 November 1965. After the April 1979 election the name Zimbabwe Rhodesia was used from June to December 1979; the Lancaster House Agreement is dated 21 December 1979 and control returned to Britain on 11-12 December 1979.

eras.polity: Zimbabwe - Bulawayo and the Matabeleland provinces
eras.note: Independence came on 18 April 1980. The Gukurahundi massacres in Matabeleland are dated early 1983 to late 1987 in one account and 1982-1987 in another; the International Association of Genocide Scholars estimates more than 20,000 deaths. Matabeleland now comprises Bulawayo, Matabeleland North and Matabeleland South provinces.

regions.label: Mashonaland and the eastern highlands
regions.sub: Harare, Mutare, Kadoma, Marondera, Bindura, Chipinge, Chiredzi

eras.polity: British South Africa Company - Fort Salisbury and Mashonaland
eras.note: The Pioneer Column occupied Mashonaland in 1890 and founded Fort Salisbury, now Harare. A revolt against the Company led by Mwari priests broke out in 1896. The name Southern Rhodesia was made official on 20 October 1898.

eras.polity: Colony of Southern Rhodesia - Mashonaland one of five provinces
eras.note: The UK annexed Southern Rhodesia on 12 September 1923, and Mashonaland became one of its five provinces. The National Archives of Zimbabwe were established in 1935 and hold the archives of the former Southern Rhodesia.

eras.polity: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, then Southern Rhodesia again
eras.note: From 1953 to 1963 the National Archives in Harare served as the central repository for the National Archives of Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
UDI was declared on 11 November 1965. In 1970 Mashonaland was divided into northern and southern halves.

eras.polity: Zimbabwe - Harare and the Mashonaland provinces
eras.note: Independence came on 18 April 1980. In 1983 Mashonaland was divided into three sectors and Harare became a separate province; governors appointed by the president have run each province since 1988. The Mashonaland provinces are Mashonaland West, Central and East, with Harare.

regions.label: Southern Namibia - Great Namaqualand and Hardap
regions.sub: Keetmanshoop, Aranos, Mariental, Lüderitz, Bethanie

eras.note: Before registers. A Nama captain, Hendrik Tseib of the Kharoǃoan, found the spring at Keetmanshoop in 1808, and the Kharoǃoan clan settled there permanently in February 1850. In the 19th century Oorlam groups led by Jonker Afrikaner gained control of grazing land.

The Rhenish Missionary Society founded a mission at Keetmanshoop in 1860; its first missionary, Johann Georg Schröder, arrived on 14 April 1866, which is marked as the town's founding date. The town is named after Johann Keetman of the Society.

Germany claimed the territory in 1884 after Adolf Lüderitz's purchase of Angra Pequena. The Nama and Herero rose in 1904, and the German genocide of both peoples is dated 1904-1907 in one account. Diamonds were found in 1908. German documents that survived the First World War were later incorporated into the National Archives of Namibia in Windhoek.

eras.polity: South African occupation and League of Nations mandate (South West Africa)
eras.note: South Africa occupied the territory in 1915 and governed it under a League of Nations mandate from 1920; the UN General Assembly ended the mandate in 1966 but South Africa kept control. The South West Africa Archives Depot, forerunner of the National Archives, was founded in 1939.
Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990. The Archives Act (No. 12 of 1992) governs the National Archives, which since 2000 have been in Windhoek's Eugène Marais Street.

regions.label: Northern Cape - Griqualand West, Namaqualand, Bushmanland
regions.sub: Kimberley, Upington, Springbok, Kuruman, Vryburg, De Aar, Prieska

eras.polity: Griqua captaincy of Klaarwater (Griquatown) - the Waterboer line
eras.note: Before registers. Griqualand West is dated to 1800 under the Griqua captain Adam Kok I, centred on Klaarwater, later Griekwastad (Griquatown). Andries Waterboer took control from 1820, and in 1834 the Cape Colony recognised his rights to his land and people.

The Keate Award went in Nicolaas Waterboer's favour in 1871 and the district was proclaimed British territory on 27 October 1871 (1871 or 1873 depending on the source). Kimberley was the capital. In July 1876 the Orange Free State received compensation for its claims. The Griqualand West Annexation Act is dated 27 July 1877.

eras.polity: Cape Colony - Griqualand West united 1880, British Bechuanaland annexed 1895
eras.note: Griqualand West was united with the Cape Colony on 18 October 1880. British Bechuanaland, formed on 30 September 1885 from Stellaland, Goshen and other territory south of the Molopo (Vryburg was Stellaland's main town), was annexed to the Cape on 16 November 1895.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa - Cape Province
eras.note: The Cape Colony became the Cape Province on 31 May 1910 at the formation of the Union. The province took in Griqualand West, British Bechuanaland and Namaqualand (Springbok).

eras.polity: Republic of South Africa - Northern Cape Province
eras.note: The Cape Province was broken up on 27 April 1994 and the Northern Cape was one of the three provinces made from it. The Orange River divides Little Namaqualand (Northern Cape) from Great Namaqualand in Namibia.

regions.label: Lesotho - Basutoland
regions.sub: Maseru, Mafeteng, Quthing, Mohale's Hoek, Teyateyaneng

eras.note: Before registers. Moshoeshoe I sought British protection during his conflict with the Orange Free State, and Britain took control of the territory in 1868.
Britain took control of Basutoland in 1868 after Moshoeshoe I asked for protection.
Rule by the Cape Colony began in 1871 and was unpopular; it led to the Gun War of 1880-1881.

eras.polity: Basutoland - British Crown colony under the High Commissioner
eras.note: The territory returned to direct Crown authority in 1884, governed through the High Commissioner and a series of British Resident Commissioners. It joined a customs union in 1891, and a National Council formed in 1903.
Basutoland became independent as the Kingdom of Lesotho on 4 October 1966.

regions.label: Eswatini - Swaziland
regions.sub: Mbabane, Manzini, Lobamba, Siteki

eras.note: Before registers. The Dlamini kings Ngwane III, Ndvungunye and Sobhuza I consolidated the kingdom from the 1740s; Mswati II reigned from 1839 to 1865 and gave the country its name. Land deals with Boer settlers in the 1840s and 1850s were disputed and their terms vague.

eras.polity: Swaziland under the Pretoria and London Conventions
eras.note: The 1881 Pretoria Convention recognised Swazi independence but reduced its territory, and the 1884 London Convention affirmed independence again. Mass concessions to European settlers followed under King Mbandzeni; after he died in 1889 a provisional administration was proclaimed on 18 December 1889.

eras.polity: South African Republic protection - Anglo-Boer War
eras.note: A convention of 1894 placed Swaziland under South African Republic protection. British forces pushed Boer commandos out of the country by 1902.

Britain made Swaziland a protectorate in 1903. A land partition decided in 1907 and carried out in 1909 gave about one-third of the land to the Swazi nation and the rest to European settlers. Bremersdorp, now Manzini, was the colonial headquarters.
Independence came on 6 September 1968. In 1973 King Sobhuza II suspended the constitution and ruled by decree until his death in 1982; the country was renamed Eswatini in 2018.

regions.label: Southern Ghana - Accra and the Gold Coast Colony
regions.sub: Accra, Cape Coast, Takoradi, Elmina, Winneba

eras.polity: Ga kingdom of Accra and the European trading forts
eras.note: Before registers. By the 15th century the Accra kingdom ruled the area from Ayawaso. A Portuguese fort was destroyed by local people in 1576, and in the 17th century the Dutch built Fort Crèvecœur (later Ussher Fort), the British James Fort and the Swedes Christiansborg.

eras.polity: Danish Gold Coast - Christiansborg beside Dutch and British forts
eras.note: Christiansborg was first captured from the Swedes in 1658 and was Denmark's capital on the coast until 1850; the Portuguese held it between 1680 and 1682. The Akwamu sacked Ayawaso between 1677 and 1681 and burned Osu and Small Accra in 1681. Dutch Accra and James Fort stood alongside.

eras.polity: British forts on the Gold Coast
eras.note: The Danish forts were sold to the United Kingdom on 30 March 1850 (another account gives 1851). The Dutch Gold Coast was purchased by Britain on 6 April 1872, though the Dutch sale is dated 1871 in another account. Britain defeated the Asante and the Gold Coast Colony was established on 24 July 1874.

eras.polity: Gold Coast Colony - Accra the capital from 1877
eras.note: Accra replaced Cape Coast as capital in 1877. Asante was annexed as a colony in 1901 (proclaimed 1902, by one account) and the Northern Territories became a protectorate in 1902; British Togoland was admitted on 27 December 1916.
The Gold Coast became independent as Ghana on 6 March 1957, with Kwame Nkrumah its first Prime Minister.

regions.label: Cape Verde - the ten islands
regions.sub: Praia, Cidade Velha, Mindelo, Sal, Boa Vista, Brava

eras.polity: Portuguese colony - Ribeira Grande (Cidade Velha) on Santiago
eras.note: The islands were found by Genoese and Portuguese navigators around 1456; António de Noli is named in the Portuguese record as the first discoverer and Diogo Gomes claimed to be the first to land on Santiago. Settlers founded Ribeira Grande, now Cidade Velha, in 1462, the first permanent European settlement in the tropics. The islands prospered from the transatlantic slave trade in the 1500s, and pirate raids, including Francis Drake's, were common.
Praia became the capital in 1770. Droughts and famines killed more than 100,000 people over the 18th and 19th centuries, and Mindelo, on São Vicente, grew into an important coaling and shipping port.

eras.polity: Portuguese colony after the abolition of slavery
eras.note: Slavery was abolished in 1864, after the morgado system was abolished in 1863. Famines in 1941-43 and 1947-48 killed an estimated 45,000 people, and forced-labour emigration to other Portuguese colonies continued.
Portugal changed the colony to an overseas province in 1951. The PAIGC was founded in 1956 by Amílcar Cabral and others.
Independence followed the 1974 Carnation Revolution; the National Assembly received the instruments of independence from Portugal on 5 July 1975. Multiparty elections were held in 1991.

regions.label: The Channel Islands - Jersey, Guernsey, Alderney, Sark
regions.sub: St Helier, St Peter Port, Alderney, Sark, Herm

eras.note: Before registers. Jersey was annexed to the Duchy of Normandy in 933 by William Longsword and stayed a Norman possession after William the Conqueror became King of England in 1066.

eras.polity: Crown dependencies - loyal to the English Crown after the loss of Normandy
eras.note: When Normandy returned to the French king in 1204 the islands stayed with the English Crown without being incorporated into England. They kept Norman customs and laws, with a Bailiff appointed by the Crown; the Channel Islands were divided administratively in 1290 and Guernsey became part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey. Before civil registration the records are parish registers.

eras.polity: Bailiwicks of Jersey and Guernsey - civil registration begins
eras.note: Civil registration began at different dates on each island: Guernsey 1840, Jersey 1842, Alderney 1850 and Sark 1915 (dates for Alderney and Sark differ by source). Guernsey marriages are an exception, with one source giving 1919; earlier marriages are in church registers.

eras.polity: German occupation of the Channel Islands
eras.note: Germany occupied the islands from 30 June 1940 (Guernsey) or 1 July 1940 (Jersey) until liberation on 9 May 1945. About 17,000 of Guernsey's 41,000 people were evacuated to England before the occupation.

eras.polity: Crown Dependencies - Bailiwicks of Jersey and Guernsey
eras.note: Jersey and Guernsey are self-governing Crown Dependencies, not part of the United Kingdom but part of the British Islands. Jersey law rests on Norman customary law, English common law and modern French civil law. Jersey Archive, in Clarence Road, St Helier, was established in 1993.

regions.label: Luxembourg - the Grand Duchy
regions.sub: Luxembourg, Echternach, Diekirch, Vianden, Grevenmacher

eras.polity: Duchy of Luxembourg - Burgundian, then Habsburg Netherlands
eras.note: The duchy passed from Burgundy to the Habsburgs in 1477, and Spain ruled it in the 17th century. The fortress of Luxembourg was repeatedly enlarged.
Austria took control in 1714. Under the Austrian Netherlands the recording of births, marriages and deaths was left to the parishes.
Revolutionary France annexed the territory in 1795. A civil registrar took over registration from June 1796; the civil registers (1796-1941) are held by the Archives nationales de Luxembourg.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Luxembourg in personal union with the Dutch king
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna made Luxembourg a grand duchy in personal union with the King of the Netherlands.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Luxembourg - sovereign state
eras.note: The 1839 Treaty of London made Luxembourg a sovereign state and gave its western, French-speaking part to Belgium (now the Belgian province of Luxembourg, capital Arlon). The 1867 crisis over a proposed sale to France ended in a treaty guaranteeing neutrality, and the Dutch royal line ended in 1890. Germany occupied Luxembourg in the First World War.
Germany invaded in 1940 and annexed the country de facto; Allied forces liberated it in 1944-45.
Luxembourg abandoned neutrality after the war and joined NATO and the United Nations.

regions.label: Scania, Blekinge and Gotland - the Danish provinces of Sweden
regions.sub: Malmö, Lund, Karlskrona, Kalmar, Visby

eras.polity: Kingdom of Denmark - Scania under the Danish crown
eras.note: Before parish registers. Scania came under the Danish king Harald Bluetooth in the mid-10th century; Lund became the archbishopric for all of Scandinavia in 1103 and Malmö received town rights about 1250.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Denmark - Scania, Blekinge and Gotland
eras.note: Valdemar Atterdag of Denmark invaded Gotland in 1361; the Teutonic Knights conquered it in 1398; in 1409 the Teutonic Grand Master sold it to Queen Margaret, it was later sold to Eric of Pomerania, and after 1449 Danish governors ruled it. The Second Treaty of Brömsebro placed Gotland under Sweden in 1645, and the Treaty of Roskilde ceded Scania, Blekinge and Halland in 1658.
Denmark ceded all its lands east of the Öresund to Sweden in the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658. Denmark occupied parts of Scania during the Scanian War (1676-1679).

The Swedish Church Law of 1686 required ministers to record births, marriages, deaths and movements in and out of the parish. Denmark briefly occupied parts of Scania again in 1710; a Swedish-Danish peace treaty of July 1720 confirmed Scania as Swedish, and Scania was divided into two counties in 1719.
The Riksarkivet database of church records covers 1686-1991. Russian forces occupied Visby on 22 April 1808 and left on 18 May during the Finnish War.

regions.label: Lower Normandy - Cotentin, Bessin and Calvados
regions.sub: Cherbourg, Valognes, Coutances, Saint-Lô, Granville, Caen

eras.note: Before registers. Charles the Bald ceded the Cotentin to Alan the Great of Brittany in 867, and Brittany lost it to the Duchy of Normandy in 933. In 1088 Duke Robert Curthose gave the Cotentin to his brother Henry, later king of England.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - Normandy annexed by Philip II
eras.note: Philip II captured mainland Normandy in 1204 and the 1259 Treaty of Paris recognised French possession. During the Hundred Years' War Edward III landed in the bay of La Hougue.
The English controlled most of Normandy from 1419 to 1450.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - province of Normandy
eras.note: The ducal ring was broken in 1469, ending the duchy on the continent. The Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts (1539) required parishes to keep baptism registers, Blois (1579) extended registration to marriages and burials, and an ordinance of 1667 provided for a second copy to be lodged with the court clerk; one source says systematic duplication began only from 1736. The naval Battle of La Hogue was fought off Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue in 1692.

eras.polity: France - departments of Manche and Calvados
eras.note: Five departments replaced the province of Normandy in 1790; Manche was created on 26 February 1790 and its capital was Coutances until 1796, then Saint-Lô. A decree of 20 September 1792 moved register-keeping from priests to mayors, and civil registers proper begin in 1793.

The D-Day landings took place on 6 June 1944, with Utah Beach on the Cotentin coast, followed by the campaign to take Cherbourg; Valognes lost many of its grand houses. Saint-Lô was largely destroyed in the war, and Coutances briefly served again as prefecture before Saint-Lô was rebuilt.

regimeNote: Five of these carry a Wikidata id and the dates Wikidata holds for them. The rest do not, and that is deliberate: fuzzy matching offered Circassia for Croatia, Audhali for Australia and Basutoland for Poland, and several of the labels here — «Aquileia · Gorizia · Frankopan», «German occupation» — are this project's own shorthand for a situation rather than the name of a state. An honest blank beats a plausible lie. data/polities-wikidata.json holds 1,857 former countries with dates as a REFERENCE for whoever authors the next region, not as something a machine should match automatically.
regimeArchivesNote: `archives` is WHICH MODERN STATE HELD THIS GROUND under that regime — the country whose flag flew over it, and whose archive inherited the paper. Habsburg is AT and HU because the Dual Monarchy filed in both capitals; Galicia is PL and UA because the border of 1945 cut it and its archives in half. It is NOT a claim about who owns the ground today, and it is not a border: it is the answer to «whose archive do I write to for these years, and whose flag was over the parish when the entry was made». A regime that left no single successor state — the Aquileia/Gorizia/Frankopan feudal centuries — carries an empty list on purpose, because a guess at which modern capital inherited a patriarchate is exactly the inference this atlas refuses elsewhere. Read by abroadFor() for the «also governed from» sources, and by eraFlagsHtml() for the flags over the selected era.
countriesNote: Derived from each ring — the vertices, the edge midpoints and the centre — rather than from the places walked inside it. A region is a piece of ground and which countries it covers is a fact about the ground, not about whether anybody has walked a parish in it yet. A country claimed by a single sampled point is dropped as a corner clipping a neighbour.
